courses.summary: The habits every technician needs before touching a customer's vehicle: working safely, using a digital multimeter correctly, finding the right service information, and following a repeatable diagnostic process.

lessons.title: Shop safety and personal protective equipment
lessons.body:
## Why safety comes first

A repair shop holds almost every hazard you can name: heavy loads overhead, spinning belts and fans, pressurized fluids, flammable vapors, toxic exhaust, and electrical systems that can deliver hundreds of amps. Experienced technicians are not fearless. They have simply built habits that keep them from getting hurt. Build those habits from your first day, and treat every vehicle as if it could move, start, or release energy without warning.

## Personal protective equipment (PPE)

PPE is your last line of defense, not your first. It only works if you wear it every time.

- **Eye protection:** Safety glasses marked ANSI Z87.1 are the minimum any time you are in the shop. Use a face shield over glasses for grinding, cutting, or work where fluids can spray.
- **Hand protection:** Nitrile gloves keep oil, fuel, and brake fluid off your skin. Cut-resistant or mechanic's gloves protect against sharp edges. Do not wear loose gloves near rotating parts.
- **Hearing protection:** Use earplugs or muffs around impact tools, air hammers, and grinders.
- **Clothing and jewelry:** Remove rings, watches, and chains. A metal ring that bridges a battery terminal to ground can heat red-hot in seconds. Tie back long hair and keep sleeves close-fitting.
- **Foot protection:** Wear safety-toe, slip-resistant shoes.

## Lifting and supporting vehicles

Falls from lifts and jacks cause some of the most serious shop injuries.

- Use the **lift points specified in the OEM service information**. Hybrid, electric, and unibody vehicles often have specific pad locations.
- After raising a vehicle slightly, stop and check that all pads contact correctly before going higher. Always lower the lift onto its **mechanical locks** before working underneath.
- **Never work under a vehicle supported only by a jack.** Use jack stands rated for the load, on firm, level ground, with the wheels chocked.
- Removing heavy components such as transmissions or fuel tanks shifts the center of gravity. Use supplemental stands as the service procedure directs.

## Running engines, rotating parts, and exhaust gas

- **Carbon monoxide** is odorless and can be lethal. Run engines indoors only with an exhaust extraction hose connected, and never in a closed bay.
- Keep hands, tools, hair, and test leads away from belts, pulleys, and fans. **Electric cooling fans can start with the key off** on many vehicles.
- Before a running test, set the parking brake, block the wheels, and place the transmission in Park or Neutral.
- Exhaust manifolds, catalytic converters, and turbochargers stay hot long after shutdown. Never open a hot cooling system; it is pressurized and can spray scalding coolant.

## Electrical and battery hazards

- Batteries can release **hydrogen gas**. Keep sparks and flames away, and make the final connection of a jump or charger away from the battery.
- When disconnecting a battery, remove the **negative cable first**; reconnect it last.
- Starter and alternator circuits carry very high current. A wrench across a positive terminal and ground can cause severe burns.
- **Orange cables** identify hybrid and EV high-voltage systems. Do not touch them unless you are trained, equipped with rated insulated gloves, and following the OEM disable procedure.
- Airbag (SRS) components can deploy if mishandled. Follow the OEM procedure for disabling the system and wait the specified time before working near modules or connectors.

## Chemicals, fire, and compressed air

- Every chemical in the shop has a **Safety Data Sheet (SDS)** describing hazards, PPE, and first aid. Know where the SDS binder or database is.
- Know where the fire extinguishers are and what classes they are rated for. Clean up fuel spills immediately.
- Under US OSHA rules, compressed air used for cleaning must be reduced below 30 psi with chip guarding and PPE. Never point an air nozzle at yourself or anyone else.

## Worked example: a quick pre-job check

You are assigned a front brake job. Before you raise the vehicle, you:

1. Remove your ring and put on safety glasses.
2. Look up the lift points for this model and position the pads.
3. Raise the vehicle a few inches, shake-check it, then raise it to working height and **lower it onto the locks**.
4. Note that the brake fluid is irritating to skin and put on nitrile gloves.

That check takes two minutes and prevents the most likely injuries on this job.

## Safety

If you are unsure how to perform a task safely, **stop and ask**. No repair is urgent enough to justify an injury. Report damaged equipment such as frayed lift cables, leaking jacks, or cracked extension cords, and tag it out of service.

## Key takeaways

- PPE is mandatory and habitual: eye protection is the minimum at all times.
- Use OEM lift points, lift locks, and rated jack stands; never trust a jack alone.
- Control carbon monoxide with exhaust extraction and respect rotating parts.
- Treat batteries, high-current circuits, orange high-voltage cables, and airbags with trained procedures.
- Use the SDS to understand chemical hazards before you use a product.

lessons.title: Hand tools, torque, and the digital multimeter
lessons.body:
## Hand tools and fastener basics

Good diagnosis and good repairs both depend on using tools correctly.

- **Use the right size and type.** A 6-point socket grips the flats of a fastener and is less likely to round it off than a 12-point socket.
- **Pull, don't push**, on wrenches whenever possible, so a slip does not drive your knuckles into sharp metal.
- **Torque matters.** Every critical fastener has a torque value and often a tightening sequence. Always use the value in the OEM service information for that vehicle; never guess.
- **Torque-to-yield (TTY) bolts** are stretched on purpose during installation. Many are one-time-use. Follow the OEM procedure, which may call for a torque value followed by an angle.
- A **torque wrench is a measuring instrument.** Have it calibrated periodically, never use it to break fasteners loose, and store a click-type wrench as its manufacturer recommends.

Torque is published in either **lb-ft** or **N·m**. One lb-ft equals about 1.356 N·m. Converting correctly is a real-world skill, and the exercises in this course let you practice it.

## The digital multimeter (DMM)

The DMM is the most important electrical diagnostic tool you will own. A typical automotive meter measures:

- **DC volts** for battery, sensor, and supply voltages
- **Ohms** for resistance of components and wires
- **Amps** for current flow, usually through a fused input
- **Continuity and diode test**
- Often **frequency, duty cycle, and min/max capture**

Most digital meters have a high input impedance (commonly 10 megohms), so they draw almost no current from the circuit being measured. That makes them safe to use on computer-controlled circuits, where an incandescent test light could draw too much current and damage a module output.

## Measuring voltage

Voltage is measured **in parallel**, with the circuit powered.

1. Set the meter to DC volts.
2. Place the black lead on a known-good ground or the battery negative terminal.
3. Touch the red lead to the test point.

Back-probe connectors from the wire side with thin back-probe pins or use terminal test adapters. **Do not pierce wire insulation** and do not force probes into terminals; spread terminals cause intermittent faults later.

## Measuring resistance

Resistance is measured with the **circuit unpowered** and the component isolated. The meter supplies its own small current, and any outside voltage gives a false reading and can damage the meter. Touch the leads together first to note lead resistance.

An important limitation: an ohmmeter pushes only a tiny current. A wire with one strand left intact can read nearly perfect on an ohmmeter yet fail under a real load. That is why voltage drop testing, covered in the Electrical course, is often the better test.

## Measuring current

Current is measured **in series**: the circuit must flow through the meter.

- Move the red lead to the amps jack and open the circuit so the meter completes it.
- **Never connect the meter leads across a voltage source while they are in the amps jack.** That creates a near short circuit and blows the meter fuse or damages the meter.
- For high currents such as starter draw, use an inductive **clamp-on amp probe** instead.

## Worked example: a lamp that will not light (illustrative values)

Picture the simple circuit in the diagram: battery, fuse, switch, lamp, and ground. The lamp is off with the switch on.

- Black lead on battery negative, red lead on the lamp's feed terminal: **12.4 V**. Power is reaching the lamp.
- Red lead moved to the lamp's ground terminal: **12.4 V** again.

Voltage on both sides of the lamp means no current is flowing, so there is no voltage drop across the lamp. The lamp filament is conducting, and the **ground path is open**. The next step is to test along the ground wire toward its ground point. Notice that no parts were replaced to reach this conclusion.

## Safety

- Keep jewelry off and use insulated tools around battery and starter circuits.
- Check the meter's **CAT safety rating**. Hybrid and EV high-voltage work requires a meter and leads rated for that use under OEM guidance, plus training.
- Inspect test leads for cracked insulation before every use.

## Key takeaways

- Look up torque values and tightening sequences in OEM service information for the specific vehicle.
- Voltage is measured in parallel on a live circuit; resistance on an unpowered, isolated component; current in series.
- An ohmmeter reading does not prove a wire can carry load current.
- Voltage readings on both sides of a load with no current flow point to an open on the ground side.
- Protect the meter, the vehicle, and yourself: correct jacks, correct range, correct probes.

lessons.title: Reading service information, TSBs, and recalls
lessons.body:
## Why service information matters

Modern vehicles differ enormously, even between model years and engine options of the same model. Specifications, wiring, test procedures, and even the meaning of some trouble codes change from vehicle to vehicle. Professional technicians do not work from memory; they **look it up every time**. Knowing how to find and read service information is as important as knowing how to use a wrench.

## Types of service information

- **OEM service information:** The manufacturer's own repair procedures, specifications, wiring diagrams, and diagnostic routines. Usually available by subscription. This is the authoritative source.
- **Aftermarket repair databases:** Compiled information from multiple manufacturers, often with added real-world repair tips. Useful, but verify critical specifications against OEM information when possible.
- **Technical Service Bulletins (TSBs):** Documents a manufacturer issues when it identifies a common problem, a revised repair procedure, updated parts, or new software.
- **Recalls and campaigns:** Safety or emissions corrections that the manufacturer must address.
- **Owner's manual and maintenance schedules:** Fluid types, service intervals, and warning light descriptions.

## Identify the vehicle precisely

Before you look anything up, confirm exactly what vehicle you have.

- **Decode the VIN.** The 17-character VIN identifies the model year and often the engine and body. Do not rely on the repair order or the customer's description alone.
- Check the **production date** on the door-jamb label. Many changes happen mid-year, and service information may split procedures by build date or VIN range.
- Note engine, transmission, and option labels in the vehicle.

## Anatomy of a diagnostic procedure

A typical OEM diagnostic procedure for a trouble code contains several parts. Read them all before you start testing.

- **Description and operation:** How the system works. Read this first when the system is unfamiliar.
- **Conditions for running the diagnostic:** The enable criteria, such as coolant temperature, engine speed, or time since start. If these are not met, the monitor never runs.
- **Conditions for setting the DTC:** What the module must see, and for how long, before it sets the code.
- **Actions taken when the DTC sets:** For example, turning on the MIL or entering a limp mode.
- **Circuit or system description and diagnostic steps:** A sequence of tests with expected results. Perform the steps in order; each step assumes the previous ones passed.

**Specifications** such as resistance, pressure, voltage, and torque appear within these procedures. Always use the value for the exact vehicle and note the units and test conditions, such as engine temperature.

## TSBs: strong clues, not proof

A TSB tells you what the manufacturer has seen on many vehicles. Search by VIN or by year, make, model, and engine, then read the **applicability** carefully: VIN ranges, build dates, and exact symptoms.

A TSB does not prove that your vehicle has that problem. It raises the probability of a cause, and you still verify with a test before performing the repair.

## Recalls

Safety recalls are corrections the manufacturer must perform, typically at no charge through its dealers. Check open recalls by VIN, for example through NHTSA's online recall lookup in the United States. An open recall can explain the customer's complaint or affect the repair you are about to perform.

## Worked example

A vehicle has the MIL on with **P0128** (coolant temperature below thermostat regulating temperature), set only during cold weather. Your search finds a TSB describing a software update that revises P0128 logic for a specific VIN range.

1. You confirm the VIN falls within the bulletin range.
2. You read the vehicle's calibration ID with a scan tool and compare it to the TSB.
3. Before updating software, you still **test the cooling system**: you watch coolant temperature rise on a cold engine and compare it to expected warm-up behavior.

If the thermostat is stuck open, the software update alone would not fix the vehicle. The TSB guided the diagnosis, and the test confirmed it.

## Safety

Service information contains the **OEM warnings and disable procedures** for airbags, hybrid and EV high-voltage systems, and other hazards. Read every warning and caution in a procedure before you begin. A warning usually describes a risk of injury; a caution usually describes a risk of damage to the vehicle.

## Key takeaways

- Look up specifications and procedures for the exact vehicle every time; never guess values.
- Decode the VIN and check the production date before selecting information.
- Read the enable criteria and setting conditions for a DTC before testing.
- TSBs and known patterns guide diagnosis, but a test must confirm the cause.
- Check for open recalls by VIN, and read all safety warnings before starting a procedure.

lessons.title: The diagnostic process: from complaint to verified repair
lessons.body:
## Why follow a process?

Replacing parts until a problem goes away is slow, expensive, and often unsuccessful. A trouble code tells you what a module detected, not which part failed. A structured process makes your diagnosis repeatable, keeps you from skipping steps under time pressure, and gives you evidence to explain the repair to the customer. The motto is simple: **test before you replace**.

## The seven-step process

### 1. Verify the complaint

Understand exactly what the customer is experiencing. Ask:

- **When** does it happen: cold start, fully warm, after a long drive?
- **How often**, and did it start suddenly or gradually?
- **Under what conditions**: speed, load, weather, road surface, A/C on or off?
- Has any recent work been done?

Then duplicate the symptom yourself. If you cannot reproduce it, you cannot prove you fixed it.

### 2. Gather information

- Scan **all modules** for DTCs, not only the engine module, and record the codes before clearing anything.
- Save the **freeze frame** data. It shows the operating conditions when a code set.
- Review service history, TSBs, and open recalls.

### 3. Inspect and check the basics

A surprising number of problems are found here. Check fluid levels and condition, battery state of charge and terminal condition, visible wiring damage, loose or cracked hoses, and signs of previous repairs or aftermarket accessories.

### 4. Analyze and form hypotheses

List the possible causes that could produce **all** of the symptoms and codes. Rank them by how likely they are and how easy they are to test. A known pattern failure makes a cause more likely, but it is still only a hypothesis.

### 5. Test to isolate the root cause

Choose tests that **separate** your hypotheses. A good test gives a different result depending on which cause is present. Write down every result, including normal ones; a pass eliminates possibilities.

### 6. Repair the root cause

Fix the cause, not only the symptom. If a fuse blew, find the chafed wire that blew it. If a sensor connector corroded, find out how water got in.

### 7. Verify the repair and document it

Operate the vehicle under the same conditions that caused the fault. Confirm the symptom is gone, no codes return, and relevant readiness monitors complete where practical. Then document the **three Cs** on the repair order:

- **Concern:** what the customer reported and what you verified
- **Cause:** what you found and the test results that proved it
- **Correction:** what you repaired or replaced

## Worked example

**Concern:** "The check engine light is on, and the car hesitates when I accelerate onto the highway."

- **Information:** The engine module has **P0171** (system too lean, bank 1). Freeze frame shows high engine load, about 2,500 RPM, and a large positive long-term fuel trim.
- **Basics:** No obvious vacuum hose damage, and fluid levels are normal.
- **Hypotheses:** A vacuum leak usually causes the largest lean error at idle, when manifold vacuum is highest. A fuel delivery problem or a mass airflow sensor that under-reports airflow usually shows up under load.
- **Testing:** Live data shows fuel trims near normal at idle but strongly positive under load, which points away from a vacuum leak. A fuel pressure and volume test shows volume falling off under load. Before condemning the pump, you check **voltage drop** on its power and ground circuits and find a heavily corroded ground connection.
- **Correction:** Repair the ground, then road test under the freeze frame conditions. Fuel trims return to normal and the code does not return.

Following the process kept a good fuel pump in the car.

## Intermittent problems

When a fault will not appear on demand, rely on freeze frame, data recording during road tests, and **wiggle tests** of wiring while monitoring data. Document the conditions carefully so the next test is focused.

## Safety

- Road tests with a scan tool are safer with a second person operating the tool. The driver's attention belongs on the road.
- Run engines indoors only with exhaust extraction connected, and keep clear of belts and cooling fans during running tests.

## Key takeaways

- Verify the complaint first; if you cannot reproduce it, you cannot verify a fix.
- Record DTCs and freeze frame before clearing anything.
- Rank hypotheses by likelihood and ease of testing, then choose tests that separate them.
- Repair the root cause and verify under the original failure conditions.
- Document the concern, cause, and correction with the test results that support them.

questions.q: A lamp does not light with its switch on. With the black meter lead on battery negative, you read battery voltage at both the lamp's feed terminal and its ground terminal. What is the most likely fault?
choices: The lamp filament is burned out
An open in the lamp's ground circuit
A blown fuse in the feed circuit
A short to ground on the feed wire
questions.explanation: Voltage on both sides of the lamp means no current is flowing, so nothing is dropped across the lamp. The filament must be conducting to pass voltage to its ground terminal, so the break is on the ground side. A burned-out filament would leave near 0 V on the ground terminal, and a blown fuse would leave near 0 V at the feed.

questions.q: Why can a wire that reads nearly 0 ohms on an ohmmeter still cause a circuit to fail?
choices: Ohmmeters only read correctly on AC circuits
Wire resistance depends on insulation color
Resistance must always be measured with the circuit powered
The ohmmeter's tiny test current can pass through a few remaining strands that cannot carry the real load current
questions.explanation: An ohmmeter pushes only a very small current. A wire with most strands broken or a corroded terminal can pass that test current easily, yet cause a large voltage drop under real load. Voltage drop testing with the circuit operating finds these faults.

questions.q: You have raised a vehicle to working height on a two-post lift. What should you do before working underneath it?
choices: Lower the lift onto its mechanical locks
Leave it held by hydraulic pressure so it can be adjusted quickly
Place a floor jack under the engine as the main support
Chock only the rear wheels
questions.explanation: Hydraulic pressure can bleed off or a seal can fail. Resting the lift on its mechanical locks is the standard practice before working underneath. Pads must also be on the OEM-specified lift points.

questions.q: A TSB describes your customer's exact symptom and the VIN falls within its range. What is the best next step?
choices: Perform the TSB repair immediately without further testing
Ignore it, because TSBs apply only to dealer repairs
Verify that the vehicle actually has the condition the TSB describes, then perform the repair if confirmed
Clear the codes and wait to see if the problem returns
questions.explanation: A TSB raises the probability of a specific cause, but it is not proof. A quick confirming test prevents unnecessary repairs when the vehicle has a different fault with similar symptoms.

questions.q: A customer reports a stumble that happens only on cold mornings. You cannot reproduce it during the afternoon. What is the best approach?
choices: Replace the part that most commonly causes stumbles
Tell the customer no problem was found and return the vehicle without notes
Keep the vehicle for a cold soak and test it cold, using freeze frame and recorded data to target the conditions
Clear all codes so the monitors can rerun
questions.explanation: You must reproduce a fault to diagnose it and to verify the repair. Testing under the conditions the customer describes, guided by freeze frame data, is the efficient path. Guessing or clearing codes destroys evidence.

questions.q: With the red test lead still in the meter's amps jack, a technician touches the leads across the battery terminals to check voltage. What happens?
choices: The meter displays battery voltage normally
The meter becomes a near short circuit across the battery, blowing its fuse or damaging the meter
The meter reads zero and nothing is harmed
The meter measures the battery's internal resistance
questions.explanation: In the amps jack, the meter has very low resistance because it is designed to be placed in series. Connecting it across a voltage source creates a near short, driving high current through the meter.

questions.q: A monitor's enable criteria require the engine to reach full operating temperature. The customer drives only a short distance in winter. What is the likely result?
choices: The monitor may not run, so a related code may not set and readiness may stay incomplete
The monitor runs more often than normal
The DTC sets immediately on every trip
The MIL flashes to indicate the monitor is waiting
questions.explanation: If the enable criteria are never met, the diagnostic never runs. That is why reading the conditions for running a diagnostic matters when you try to reproduce a code or confirm a repair.

questions.q: The service information lists a torque value in N·m, but your torque wrench reads only in lb-ft. What should you do?
choices: Use the same number on the lb-ft scale
Tighten until it feels similar to nearby fasteners
Use a typical value you remember from another vehicle
Convert accurately using 1 lb-ft equals about 1.356 N·m, or use a wrench with an N·m scale
questions.explanation: The same number means very different clamping force in the two units. Convert carefully or use a wrench that reads the published unit. Values should always come from the OEM information for that vehicle.

questions.q: Which entry belongs on the 'Cause' line of a repair order written with the three Cs?
choices: Customer states the car hesitates when merging onto the highway
Repaired fuel pump ground connection
Fuel pump ground connection corroded; voltage drop test showed excessive drop on the ground side under load
Road tested; no codes returned
questions.explanation: The cause states what was found and the evidence that proved it. The first choice is the concern, the second is the correction, and the fourth is verification.

questions.q: Why is the negative battery cable normally disconnected first?
choices: If the wrench touches the body while loosening the negative terminal, no short circuit is created
The negative terminal carries more current
It keeps the module memory alive
The negative terminal is where hydrogen gas is released
questions.explanation: The body is connected to the negative terminal. Once the negative cable is off, a wrench touching the positive terminal and the body completes no circuit. Loosening the positive first risks a dead short if the wrench touches metal.

flashcards.back: About 1.356 N·m.
Technical Service Bulletin: a manufacturer document about a known issue, revised procedure, updated part, or software. A strong clue, not proof.
The conditions that must be met before a module runs a diagnostic monitor, such as temperature, speed, or time since start.

flashcards.front: The three Cs of a repair order
flashcards.back: Concern, Cause, Correction.

flashcards.front: What is the first step of the diagnostic process?
flashcards.back: Verify the complaint: understand it and reproduce it.

flashcards.front: What should you record before clearing any codes?
flashcards.back: All DTCs from all modules and the freeze frame data.

courses.title: Engine Operation and Mechanical Testing
courses.summary: How a four-stroke engine makes power and how to prove its mechanical health with compression, running compression, and cylinder leakage tests, plus how valve timing and variable valve timing systems work and fail.

lessons.title: The four-stroke cycle and engine construction
lessons.body:
## The engine as an air pump

A gasoline engine is a controlled air pump. It draws air in, adds the right amount of fuel, compresses the mixture, ignites it, and pushes the burned gases out. Every cylinder needs the same things to make its share of power:

- **Air** in the right amount
- **Fuel** in the right amount
- **Spark** of sufficient energy at the right time
- **Compression**, which requires good sealing by rings, valves, and the head gasket
- **Correct timing** between the crankshaft and camshafts

When one cylinder misbehaves, a good diagnostic question is: *which of these is missing?*

## The four strokes

A stroke is one movement of the piston from top dead center (**TDC**) to bottom dead center (**BDC**) or back.

1. **Intake:** The intake valve opens and the piston moves down. The falling pressure in the cylinder draws in air, or an air-fuel mixture on port-injected engines.
2. **Compression:** Both valves close and the piston moves up, squeezing the mixture into a small space. Compression raises its pressure and temperature, which makes combustion more effective.
3. **Power:** Near the top of the compression stroke, the spark plug fires. The burning mixture expands rapidly and forces the piston down. This is the only stroke that produces work.
4. **Exhaust:** The exhaust valve opens and the piston moves up, pushing burned gases out.

One complete cycle takes **two crankshaft revolutions (720 degrees)**. The camshaft turns at **half crankshaft speed**, so it opens each valve once per cycle. Near TDC between the exhaust and intake strokes, both valves are briefly open; this is called **valve overlap**, and it helps the exhaust flow draw in the fresh charge.

## Major components

- **Cylinder block:** Houses the cylinders, coolant passages, and main bearings.
- **Crankshaft:** Converts the pistons' up-and-down motion into rotation.
- **Connecting rods and pistons:** Pistons carry **compression rings** that seal combustion pressure and an **oil control ring** that scrapes oil from the cylinder wall.
- **Cylinder head:** Contains the combustion chambers, valves, valve seats, springs, and on most modern engines the camshafts. Designs include overhead valve (pushrod), single overhead cam, and dual overhead cam.
- **Head gasket:** Seals combustion pressure, coolant, and oil passages between the block and head.
- **Timing drive:** A chain, belt, or gear set that keeps the camshafts synchronized with the crankshaft.
- **Lubrication and cooling systems:** An oil pump and galleries feed bearings and the valvetrain; coolant jackets carry heat away.

## Key terms and a worked example

- **Bore:** cylinder diameter. **Stroke:** distance the piston travels from TDC to BDC.
- **Displacement:** swept volume of one cylinder multiplied by the number of cylinders.
- **Compression ratio:** (swept volume + clearance volume) divided by clearance volume.

*Example (illustrative numbers):* A cylinder has a bore of 8.6 cm and a stroke of 8.6 cm.

- Swept volume = 0.7854 × 8.6 × 8.6 × 8.6 ≈ 500 cm³
- Four such cylinders ≈ 2,000 cm³, or a 2.0 L engine
- With a clearance volume of 50 cm³, compression ratio = (500 + 50) ÷ 50 = **11:1**

## Interference and non-interference engines

In an **interference engine**, the valves and pistons occupy the same space at different times. If the timing belt or chain fails or jumps, valves can hit pistons and bend. That is why timing belt replacement intervals in the OEM maintenance schedule matter, and why a no-start after a timing drive failure calls for a compression or leakage test before anything else is replaced.

## Connecting theory to diagnosis

Understanding the cycle tells you what to test:

- A cylinder that cannot seal cannot build compression, so its power stroke is weak. Compression and leakage tests measure sealing.
- Incorrect cam timing changes when the valves open, which affects compression, manifold vacuum, and cam/crank correlation data.
- A misfire on one cylinder is narrowed down by checking that cylinder's air, fuel, spark, and compression separately.

## Safety

- When rotating the engine by hand, use the crankshaft bolt and turn it **in the normal direction of rotation** unless the service information says otherwise. Turning some engines backward can disturb the timing drive or its tensioner.
- Keep hands clear of belts, pulleys, and cooling fans, and make sure no one can crank the engine while you work on it.

## Key takeaways

- Each cylinder needs air, fuel, spark, compression, and correct timing to make power.
- The four-stroke cycle takes two crankshaft turns; the camshaft turns at half crankshaft speed.
- Rings, valves, and the head gasket seal the cylinder; testing sealing is a core engine diagnostic skill.
- Timing drive failures on interference engines can bend valves, so test before replacing parts.
- Use the cycle to ask focused questions about what a weak cylinder is missing.

lessons.title: Cranking and running compression tests
lessons.body:
## What a compression test tells you

A compression test measures how much pressure each cylinder builds as the engine cranks. It is a **sealing test**: rings, valves, and the head gasket must all seal for the cylinder to hold pressure. It does not tell you which part is leaking, but it quickly shows whether a cylinder has a mechanical problem and whether further testing is needed.

## Preparing for a cranking compression test

Consistent conditions give comparable readings.

- **Warm engine**, unless the service information specifies otherwise. Warm parts seal more consistently.
- **Fully charged battery.** Cranking speed strongly affects readings; a slow crank reads low on every cylinder.
- **Disable fuel and ignition** as the service information directs, so the engine cannot start or flood, and coils do not fire into open circuits.
- **Remove all spark plugs**, so the engine cranks evenly. Note the condition of each plug as you remove it.
- **Hold the throttle wide open** so the cylinders can fill with air. Some electronic throttle systems require a specific procedure; check the service information.

## Procedure

1. Thread the gauge hose into the spark plug hole hand-tight.
2. Crank the engine through the same number of compression strokes for every cylinder, typically four to six puffs.
3. Record the **first-puff reading** and the **final reading**.
4. Release the gauge and repeat for each cylinder.

## Interpreting the results

The absolute value depends on the engine design; compare it to the OEM specification when one is published. The most useful information comes from **comparing cylinders to each other**.

- **All cylinders close together:** A common guideline is that all cylinders should be within about 10–15% of each other (general guideline — verify against OEM specification).
- **One cylinder low:** Suspect rings, a valve, or the head gasket at that cylinder.
- **Two adjacent cylinders low:** Suspect a head gasket leak between them.
- **Zero or near zero:** Suspect a badly burned or bent valve, a holed piston, or a failed valvetrain part.
- **Higher than normal:** Carbon buildup can reduce clearance volume and raise compression.
- **First puff:** A low first puff that builds up strongly on later puffs often points toward ring sealing, while a low first puff that barely builds often points toward a valve (general guideline — verify with further testing).

## The wet test

If a cylinder reads low, add a small squirt of engine oil through the plug hole and retest.

- **Reading rises significantly:** The oil temporarily sealed the rings, so the rings or cylinder walls are the likely leak.
- **Reading barely changes:** Suspect a valve or head gasket.

The wet test is less reliable on horizontally opposed engines, where oil pools on one side of the cylinder. Use no more oil than necessary; liquid does not compress.

## Worked example (illustrative values)

A four-cylinder engine has a misfire code for cylinder 3. Cranking compression readings:

- Cylinder 1: 175 psi
- Cylinder 2: 170 psi
- Cylinder 3: 110 psi dry, 118 psi wet
- Cylinder 4: 172 psi

Cylinder 3 is roughly 35% below the others, far outside the general guideline. The wet test barely raises it, so the rings are less likely. The next step is a **cylinder leakage test** on cylinder 3 to hear where the air escapes: intake, exhaust, or the cooling system.

## Running compression and relative compression

- **Running compression test:** The gauge is connected to a cylinder with the engine idling, then the throttle is snapped. Running readings are much lower than cranking readings because the throttle restricts cylinder filling at idle. This test reveals **breathing problems**, such as a worn cam lobe or a lifter that does not fully open a valve, that can pass a cranking test.
- **Relative compression test:** A scope and current clamp, or some scan tools, measure starter current while cranking with fuel disabled. Each compression stroke causes a current peak; a weak cylinder causes a lower peak. It is a fast screening test that does not require removing spark plugs.

## Safety

- The engine will crank while you work near belts and the fan. Keep hands and hoses clear.
- **Disable fuel and ignition** before cranking. Coils fired with no plug connected can produce dangerous voltage and can damage the coil or driver.
- Parts are hot on a warm engine. Remove plugs carefully, and follow the service information on removing plugs from warm aluminum cylinder heads.
- Run the engine for a running compression test only with exhaust extraction.

## Key takeaways

- Compression testing measures cylinder sealing; compare cylinders to each other and to the OEM specification.
- Control the variables: warm engine, charged battery, all plugs out, throttle open, fuel and ignition disabled.
- A wet test helps separate ring leakage from valve or head gasket leakage.
- A low cylinder calls for a leakage test to pinpoint the leak path before any parts are replaced.
- Running and relative compression tests find problems a cranking test can miss, or screen cylinders quickly.

lessons.title: Cylinder leakage (leak-down) testing
lessons.body:
## Compression tells you how much; leakage tells you where

A compression test shows that a cylinder is weak. A **cylinder leakage test**, often called a leak-down test, shows **where** the pressure escapes. Together they turn a vague "low compression" finding into a specific, provable cause.

## How the tester works

The tester feeds regulated shop air through a calibrated orifice into the cylinder while the piston sits at **top dead center on the compression stroke**, with both valves closed. Two gauges (or one gauge with a calibrated scale) compare the pressure supplied with the pressure the cylinder holds, and the tester displays the difference as **percent leakage**. You then listen and look for where the air goes.

## Setting up the test

1. Warm the engine if practical, then shut it off. Warm parts seal the way they do in service.
2. Remove the spark plug from the cylinder being tested. Removing all plugs makes rotating the engine easier.
3. Bring the cylinder to **TDC on its compression stroke**. Use a TDC whistle, watch the piston with a borescope, or observe the valves. Both valves must be closed.
4. Calibrate the tester according to its instructions, usually by setting the regulator to a specified reading with the outlet blocked.
5. Connect the hose and apply air. **Hold the crankshaft** with a wrench on the crank bolt if the engine tends to rotate.

## Where the air goes

Listen and look at these points while the cylinder is pressurized:

- **Throttle body or intake:** leaking **intake valve**.
- **Tailpipe:** leaking **exhaust valve**.
- **Oil fill opening, dipstick tube, or PCV:** air passing the **rings or piston**. A small amount here is normal.
- **Bubbles in the coolant** at the radiator or reservoir (engine cool, cap removed): **head gasket or a cracked head or block**.
- **Adjacent cylinder's spark plug hole:** **head gasket** leak between cylinders.

A stethoscope hose or a length of tubing held at each point helps you find faint leaks.

## Interpreting the percentage

Leak-down testers use different orifice sizes, so readings from two different testers are **not directly comparable**. Compare cylinders on the same tester.

- A well-sealed cylinder commonly shows low leakage, often under about 10%. Readings above roughly 20–30%, or one cylinder far higher than the rest, warrant investigation (general guideline — verify against OEM specification and the tester manufacturer's instructions).
- The **leak path matters more than the number**. Ten percent through the rings on a high-mileage engine may be acceptable; any steady bubbling in the coolant is not.

## Worked example (illustrative values)

Continuing from the compression lesson, cylinder 3 read low on a cranking test and barely responded to the wet test.

- Leakage on cylinders 1, 2, and 4: about 8% each, with a faint hiss at the oil fill.
- Leakage on cylinder 3: about 45%, with a strong hiss at the **tailpipe**.

The exhaust valve on cylinder 3 is not sealing. Before condemning the cylinder head, consider what holds a valve open. On engines with adjustable valve lash, **tight valve clearance** can hold a valve slightly open, and the lash closes up as valves and seats wear. Checking lash per the OEM procedure takes far less time than removing the head. If the lash is correct, a burned valve or seat damage is the likely cause, confirmed during head disassembly.

## Common mistakes

- Testing with the piston not at TDC. One valve may be partly open, giving a false leak through the intake or exhaust.
- Comparing percentages across different testers or against a number from another tool.
- Removing the radiator cap on a hot engine to look for bubbles.
- Forgetting that some air past the rings is normal.

## Safety

- **The engine can rotate suddenly** when air is applied if the piston is not exactly at TDC. Keep hands and tools clear of belts, pulleys, and the fan, and secure the crankshaft with a wrench.
- Use regulated shop air and inspect hoses and fittings. A disconnected hose under pressure can whip.
- **Do not open a hot cooling system.** Let the engine cool before removing the cap to watch for bubbles; hot, pressurized coolant can erupt and scald.

## Key takeaways

- A leakage test pinpoints the leak path: intake, exhaust, rings, head gasket, or cooling system.
- The piston must be at TDC on the compression stroke with both valves closed.
- Compare cylinders on the same tester; the location of the leak matters more than the exact percentage.
- Look for simple causes, such as tight valve lash, before recommending major repairs.
- Secure the crankshaft and never open a hot, pressurized cooling system.

lessons.title: Valve timing and variable valve timing
lessons.body:
## Mechanical valve timing

The camshafts must stay synchronized with the crankshaft so each valve opens and closes at the correct point in the cycle. A timing chain, belt, or gear set maintains that relationship, and timing marks on the sprockets and covers are used to set it during assembly.

When base timing is wrong, the symptoms follow from the four-stroke cycle:

- **Retarded cam timing** closes the intake valve late, so some mixture is pushed back out. Expect reduced compression, low manifold vacuum, and poor low-speed power.
- **Timing off by several teeth** can cause a no-start and, on interference engines, valve damage.
- The engine module compares camshaft and crankshaft position signals. When the relationship falls outside its limits, it can set a **cam/crank correlation code**, such as P0016 (crankshaft position–camshaft position correlation, bank 1 sensor A).

**Timing chain stretch** is a common wear condition. Chains do not literally stretch; wear in the pins and bushings lengthens the chain, which gradually retards cam timing.

## How variable valve timing works

Fixed cam timing is a compromise. Variable valve timing (VVT) lets the engine module shift cam timing while the engine runs to improve power, fuel economy, and emissions. Changing valve overlap can also provide internal exhaust gas recirculation.

A typical hydraulic VVT system includes:

- **Cam phaser:** A vane-type actuator on the camshaft that rotates the cam relative to its sprocket.
- **Oil control valve (VVT solenoid):** A pulse-width-modulated valve that routes pressurized engine oil to advance or retard the phaser.
- **Camshaft position sensor:** Reports actual cam position so the module can compare it with the desired position.
- **Engine oil:** The working fluid. Oil level, pressure, cleanliness, and viscosity directly affect phaser response.

Some engines use electrically driven cam phasers or variable valve lift systems. The diagnostic logic is similar: command a change, then verify the response.

## VVT faults and their causes

Generic codes in the P0010–P0025 range cover camshaft actuator circuit and timing performance faults. Common causes include:

- Low oil level, wrong viscosity, or sludged oil
- A clogged oil control valve screen or filter
- An open or shorted solenoid circuit, or a failed solenoid
- A sticking phaser or a worn phaser locking pin
- Timing chain stretch or a jumped timing chain
- A faulty cam or crank sensor, or a damaged reluctor

## Testing before replacing

1. **Check the oil first.** Verify level, condition, and that the viscosity matches the OEM specification.
2. **Compare desired and actual cam position** in scan data during idle, acceleration, and cruise. A slow or absent response points toward oil supply, the solenoid, or the phaser.
3. **Command the solenoid** with scan tool bidirectional controls at idle, if supported. When the cam moves significantly, idle quality should change noticeably. No change suggests the command is not reaching the phaser.
4. **Test the circuit.** Check solenoid power, the module's control signal on a scope, and solenoid resistance per OEM specification.
5. **Verify base mechanical timing** before replacing a phaser. Use the OEM procedure, cam and crank position data, or a scope comparison of cam and crank signals against a known-good waveform.

## Worked example

A high-mileage engine sets a cam/crank correlation code for bank 1. The oil level and condition are acceptable.

- At idle, with the phasers in their base position, scan data shows **both** the intake and exhaust cams retarded by a similar amount compared with known-good data.
- A scope capture of cam and crank signals confirms that both cam signals lag the crank signal.

One phaser or solenoid would affect only its own camshaft. Both cams being equally retarded points to the component they share: the **timing chain**. Measuring chain wear or checking timing mark alignment per the service information confirms the diagnosis before the timing components are replaced.

## Safety

- Bidirectional VVT commands can make the engine idle roughly or stall. Keep clear of belts and fans, and make sure the vehicle is in Park or Neutral with the parking brake set.
- Engine oil and timing covers can be very hot after running. Allow the engine to cool before opening the oil system or checking timing marks.

## Key takeaways

- Correct crank-to-cam timing is essential for compression, vacuum, and cam/crank correlation.
- VVT uses engine oil and a PWM solenoid to move a cam phaser; oil condition is part of every VVT diagnosis.
- Compare desired and actual cam position and use bidirectional commands to test the system's response.
- Verify base mechanical timing before replacing phasers or solenoids.
- Look for the common factor: a fault affecting every camshaft points to a shared component.

questions.q: A cranking compression test shows two adjacent cylinders reading well below the others, which are all close together. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Worn piston rings in both cylinders
Burned exhaust valves in both cylinders
A head gasket leak between the two cylinders
Retarded camshaft timing
questions.explanation: Two neighboring cylinders failing at the same time share one likely leak path: the head gasket between them. Rings or valves failing identically in adjacent cylinders is less likely, and cam timing errors affect all cylinders on that camshaft.

questions.q: A low cylinder rises substantially when a small amount of oil is added and the compression test is repeated. Where is the leak most likely?
choices: Past the piston rings or cylinder wall
Through the exhaust valve
Through the intake valve
Through the head gasket into the cooling system
questions.explanation: Oil temporarily seals the gap between the rings and the cylinder wall. If the reading rises, the rings were the leak. Valve or head gasket leaks are not sealed by oil, so the reading barely changes.

questions.q: During a cylinder leakage test with the piston at TDC on compression, air is clearly heard at the throttle body. What is leaking?
choices: The exhaust valve
The piston rings
The head gasket into a coolant passage
The intake valve
questions.explanation: Air escaping into the intake tract can only get there past the intake valve. Exhaust valve leaks are heard at the tailpipe, ring leaks at the oil fill, and coolant-side leaks show as bubbles in the coolant.

questions.q: Why should the battery be fully charged and all spark plugs removed for a cranking compression test?
choices: To prevent the engine from flooding
Cranking speed affects the readings, so every cylinder should be tested at the same, normal cranking speed
To allow oil pressure to build before testing
To reset the engine module's adaptive values
questions.explanation: A slow or uneven crank lowers the readings. Removing all plugs and using a charged battery keeps cranking speed consistent, so the cylinders can be compared fairly.

questions.q: Why shouldn't you compare a leakage percentage from your tester with a reading taken on a different brand of tester?
choices: Shop air pressure always fluctuates between tests
Gauge accuracy depends on ambient temperature
Testers use different calibrated orifice sizes, so the same cylinder can read differently on each
Leakage testers only measure ring leakage
questions.explanation: The percentage depends on the tester's internal orifice. Compare cylinders on the same tester and focus on the leak path. Any absolute limits come from the OEM or the tester manufacturer.

questions.q: All cylinders pass a cranking compression test, but one cylinder has much lower running compression than the others and misfires at idle. What should you suspect?
choices: A valvetrain problem, such as a worn cam lobe or a lifter that does not fully open a valve
Worn piston rings
A cracked head leaking combustion gas into the coolant
A weak battery
questions.explanation: A cranking test mainly checks sealing at low speed. Problems with how the cylinder breathes while running, such as insufficient valve lift, often pass a cranking test but show up in a running compression test.

questions.q: With the phasers in their base position, scan and scope data show both the intake and exhaust camshafts retarded by a similar amount relative to the crankshaft. What is the most likely cause?
choices: A failed intake VVT solenoid
A sticking exhaust cam phaser
Low engine oil pressure
Timing chain wear or a jumped chain affecting both camshafts
questions.explanation: A solenoid or phaser fault affects only its own camshaft. When both cams are equally retarded, the shared component, the timing chain, is the likely cause. Confirm it with the OEM timing verification procedure before replacing parts.

questions.q: A VVT performance code has set. What should you check first?
choices: Install a new cam phaser
Oil level, condition, and viscosity
Install a new VVT solenoid
Clear the code and road test the vehicle
questions.explanation: Hydraulic VVT systems use engine oil as their working fluid. Low, sludged, or incorrect-viscosity oil is a common cause and takes minutes to check.

questions.q: Why does the camshaft sprocket have twice as many teeth as the crankshaft sprocket on a four-stroke engine?
choices: To increase camshaft torque
To reduce timing chain wear
Each valve opens once per cycle, and one cycle takes two crankshaft revolutions
To make room for a cam phaser
questions.explanation: The four strokes take 720 degrees of crankshaft rotation. The camshaft must turn once in that time, so it runs at half crankshaft speed.

questions.q: During a leakage test you hear air at the tailpipe, but you are not certain the piston was at TDC on compression. What should you do?
choices: Condemn the exhaust valve
Confirm the piston is at TDC on the compression stroke with both valves closed, then retest
Increase the regulator pressure until the leak stops
Skip that cylinder and test the next one in the firing order
questions.explanation: If the piston is not at TDC on compression, the exhaust valve may be partly open, creating a false leak. Reposition the piston, secure the crankshaft, and retest before drawing conclusions.

courses.title: Fuel Systems and Fuel Trim
courses.summary: How return, returnless, and direct injection fuel systems deliver and control fuel, how to test pressure and volume, how to read short- and long-term fuel trims, and how to test fuel injectors.

lessons.title: Fuel delivery systems: return, returnless, and direct injection
lessons.body:
## What the fuel system must do

The fuel system has one job: deliver **clean fuel, at the pressure the injectors need, in enough volume**, under every operating condition from a cold start to wide-open throttle. The engine module calculates how much fuel each cylinder needs and sets injector pulse width assuming the pressure is correct. If pressure or volume is wrong, every fuel calculation is wrong.

Most systems share these parts: a tank, an in-tank electric pump module with an inlet strainer, a filter (in the tank module or inline), supply lines, a fuel rail, injectors, and some method of **pressure regulation**. The main differences between system types are where pressure is regulated and whether excess fuel returns to the tank.

## Return-type systems

In a return system, the pump supplies more fuel than the engine needs.

- A **pressure regulator** on or near the fuel rail holds rail pressure and sends excess fuel back to the tank through a **return line**.
- The regulator is usually **referenced to intake manifold vacuum**. At idle, high vacuum lowers rail pressure; under load, low vacuum raises it. This keeps the pressure difference across the injector nearly constant, so injector flow depends mainly on pulse width.
- Drawback: fuel circulating past the hot engine returns to the tank warm, which increases fuel vapor.

## Mechanical returnless systems

Here the regulator sits in the **tank module**, and only one line runs to the rail.

- Excess fuel returns to the tank inside the module, so less heated fuel reaches the tank.
- Rail pressure is not vacuum referenced. The engine module compensates for changing manifold pressure in its injector pulse width calculation.
- A pulsation damper on the rail is common.

## Electronic returnless systems

An electronic returnless system adds a **fuel rail pressure sensor** and controls **pump speed**.

- The engine module, often through a separate fuel pump control module, varies pump speed with a pulse-width-modulated signal to hold a target pressure.
- Target pressure may change with operating conditions.
- Scan data usually shows **desired and actual fuel pressure**, which makes diagnosis easier.

## Gasoline direct injection (GDI)

Direct injection sprays fuel directly into the combustion chamber, which requires far higher pressure.

- **Low-pressure side:** An in-tank lift pump, usually electronic returnless, feeds the engine.
- **High-pressure side:** A mechanical pump driven by a camshaft lobe raises pressure to levels many times higher than port injection. A solenoid-controlled valve in the pump regulates rail pressure, and a rail pressure sensor provides feedback.
- Some engines use **both port and direct injectors** to combine the advantages of each.

## Pump control

The engine module controls pump power, commonly through a relay or a pump control module. Many systems run the pump briefly at key-on to prime the system, then shut it off unless the engine is cranking or running. Some vehicles also cut the pump after a collision signal or through an inertia switch.

## Worked example: identify the system before testing

A vehicle arrives with a lean code. Before connecting any gauge, identify the system type:

- **One line at the rail, no regulator on the rail:** returnless.
- **Scan data lists a fuel rail pressure PID and a desired pressure:** electronic returnless, so you can compare desired and actual pressure before touching a fitting.
- **A high-pressure pump on the cylinder head and heavy steel lines to the rail:** GDI. The high-pressure side is tested with scan data, not a gauge.

Knowing the system type tells you what normal behavior looks like and which tests are safe and meaningful. Always confirm the configuration and specifications in the service information for that vehicle.

## Safety

- Fuel systems hold pressure after shutdown. **Relieve pressure per the OEM procedure** before opening any fitting, and wrap fittings with a shop towel to catch residual fuel.
- Gasoline vapor is heavier than air and ignites easily. Keep sparks, drop lights, and open flames away, and have a suitable fire extinguisher nearby.
- **Never loosen a GDI high-pressure fitting with the engine running.** Follow the OEM procedure for the high-pressure side; many manufacturers require new high-pressure lines or fittings after removal.
- Wear eye protection and clean up spills immediately.

## Key takeaways

- Return systems regulate at the rail and often reference manifold vacuum; returnless systems regulate in the tank or by pump speed.
- Electronic returnless and GDI systems provide rail pressure data, often with desired and actual values.
- GDI adds a cam-driven high-pressure pump; test the high-pressure side with scan data, not gauges.
- Identify the system type before testing so you know what normal looks like.
- Relieve pressure per OEM procedure and control ignition sources whenever you open a fuel system.

lessons.title: Fuel pressure and volume testing
lessons.body:
## Pressure is not the whole story

A fuel pump can build normal pressure at idle, when the engine needs very little fuel, and still fail to keep up at highway load. Think of a garden hose with a partial kink: close the nozzle and the gauge reads full pressure, but open it and the flow is weak. That is why fuel delivery testing checks **pressure, volume, and pressure under load**, not a single idle reading.

## Test 1: Pressure at key-on, idle, and under load

1. Relieve system pressure and connect a gauge to the test port, or use the rail pressure PID on systems with a pressure sensor.
2. **Key on, engine off:** The pump primes. Compare the reading with the OEM specification.
3. **Idle:** On a vacuum-referenced return system, pressure should rise when the vacuum hose is removed from the regulator. Fuel in that vacuum hose indicates a leaking regulator diaphragm.
4. **Under load:** Record pressure during a road test or a loaded snap. Pressure that falls as demand rises points to a supply problem.

On **electronic returnless** systems, compare **desired and actual pressure** and watch the pump command. A pump that needs an unusually high command to reach target pressure may be worn or fed through a restriction or high-resistance circuit.

## Test 2: Residual pressure (hold test)

Watch the gauge after shutdown. Pressure should hold for the time given in the service information. A rapid drop suggests:

- A leaking **check valve** in the pump
- A leaking **injector**
- A leaking **pressure regulator**

To separate them, use proper **line blocking adapters or shutoff valves**, not pliers, to isolate the supply side from the rail. If pressure holds with the supply blocked, the leak is back toward the pump. Low residual pressure often causes long cranking after the vehicle sits.

## Test 3: Volume

Volume testing measures how much fuel the system delivers in a set time into an approved, graduated container. Compare the result with the OEM specification and procedure. A pump with normal pressure but low volume cannot support high engine load.

## Test 4: The pump's electrical health

A pump is a DC motor. It can only perform as well as its power supply allows.

- **Voltage drop:** Measure voltage drop on the pump's power and ground circuits **while the pump runs**. Low voltage at the pump reduces its speed and output.
- **Current ramp:** A low-amp current probe and scope show each commutator segment as a small hump in the current waveform. Missing or irregular humps suggest worn brushes or commutator segments. Unusually high current can indicate a binding pump or a restriction; unusually low current can indicate high circuit resistance. Compare with a known-good pattern.

## GDI systems

Test the **low-pressure side first**. The high-pressure pump cannot perform correctly if its supply is low. Use scan data for low-side pressure, if a sensor is present, and for high-side desired versus actual pressure. Do not install gauges on the high-pressure side.

## Worked example (illustrative values)

A vehicle with a returnless system sets a lean code under load.

- Key-on and idle pressure are within the OEM specification.
- During a road test, pressure falls steadily as load increases.
- With the pump running under load, the battery measures 14.2 V, but the pump connector measures only 10.1 V between its power and ground terminals.

That is a **loss of about 4 V** somewhere in the pump circuit. Voltage drop testing along the power side finds a heat-damaged terminal at the pump module connector. After repairing the connector, pressure holds under load and the lean condition is gone. The pump itself was never the problem, and a pump replaced without fixing the connector would likely have failed again.

## Safety

- Relieve pressure per the OEM procedure before connecting or disconnecting gauges, and catch residual fuel with a shop towel.
- **Never route a fuel gauge hose into the passenger compartment.** For road tests, secure the gauge outside, clear of hot and moving parts, or use a pressure transducer or scan data.
- Energize the pump only by the OEM method or with a **fused jumper**. An unfused jumper across a relay socket can cause a high-current short.
- Keep clear of belts and fans during running tests, and keep ignition sources away from any open fuel system.

## Key takeaways

- Test pressure at key-on, idle, and under load; idle pressure alone does not prove adequate delivery.
- A residual pressure drop points to a check valve, injector, or regulator leak; isolate with blocking tools.
- Volume testing proves the pump can supply enough fuel for high load.
- Check the pump's voltage supply under load before condemning the pump.
- On GDI systems, verify the low-pressure side before diagnosing the high-pressure side.

lessons.title: Fuel trims explained
lessons.body:
## What fuel trim is

The engine module calculates a **base fuel quantity** from measured airflow (a MAF sensor, or manifold pressure and engine speed) and its target air-fuel ratio. For gasoline without ethanol, the chemically correct ratio is about 14.7:1. Real engines drift from the calculation because of wear, sensor tolerance, fuel quality, and leaks. **Fuel trim is the correction** the module applies, based on oxygen or air-fuel ratio sensor feedback, to keep the mixture on target.

## Short-term and long-term trim

- **Short-term fuel trim (STFT):** An immediate correction that changes many times per second in response to the upstream oxygen or air-fuel sensor.
- **Long-term fuel trim (LTFT):** A learned correction. When STFT stays on one side of zero, the module moves LTFT so STFT can return near zero. On many systems, LTFT is stored separately for different speed and load ranges and is retained after the key is off.

Both are shown as percentages:

- **Positive trim:** The module is **adding** fuel because the sensor reports a lean mixture.
- **Negative trim:** The module is **removing** fuel because the sensor reports a rich mixture.

**Total fuel trim** is approximately STFT plus LTFT. As a rule of thumb, total fuel trim beyond roughly ±10% generally warrants investigation (general guideline — verify against OEM specification). The thresholds that set lean or rich codes are defined by the manufacturer.

## Closed loop is required

Trim corrections apply only in **closed loop**. During cold starts, wide-open throttle, and deceleration fuel cutoff, the module runs in open loop and trims are not actively correcting. Check the **fuel system status** PID before interpreting trims.

## Reading trims to find the cause

Record trims at **idle**, at about **2,500 RPM with no load**, and during a **steady loaded cruise**. The pattern across those conditions is more useful than any single number.

- **Lean at idle, near normal at higher RPM:** Classic **vacuum leak**. Unmetered air is a large share of total airflow at idle and a small share at higher airflow.
- **Near normal at idle, increasingly lean with load:** Suspect **fuel delivery**: low pressure or volume, a restricted filter, or restricted injectors.
- **Lean at all speeds:** Suspect airflow measurement, such as a contaminated MAF sensor, or low fuel pressure. Compare MAF readings with known-good data.
- **Negative (rich) trims:** Suspect leaking injectors, excessive fuel pressure, a purge valve stuck open, or fuel diluting the engine oil.

## Compare the banks

On engines with two banks, each has its own trim.

- **Both banks lean:** Look for a **common cause**, such as fuel pressure, the MAF sensor, or a leak that affects the whole intake.
- **One bank lean:** Look for something **specific to that bank**, such as an intake leak at that bank's runners, an injector problem, or an exhaust leak ahead of that bank's upstream sensor.

An exhaust leak ahead of the upstream sensor can draw in outside air, so the sensor reports lean and the module adds fuel even though the engine is not actually lean.

## Worked example (illustrative values)

A vehicle has a lean code for bank 1. Warm engine, closed loop:

- **Idle:** STFT +6%, LTFT +16%, total **+22%**
- **2,500 RPM:** STFT +1%, LTFT +4%, total **+5%**

The correction shrinks as airflow increases, which is the signature of unmetered air. A **smoke test** of the intake finds a cracked PCV hose. After the repair, idle total trim returns near zero.

Compare a different vehicle: trims are near 0% at idle but reach **+20%** on both banks during a loaded cruise. That pattern points away from a vacuum leak and toward **fuel delivery**, so the next step is a pressure and volume test under load.

## Common mistakes

- Replacing an oxygen sensor because a lean code mentions the system. The sensor is usually reporting correctly; it is the messenger.
- Reading trims in open loop.
- Looking only at STFT. A large LTFT with a small STFT means the module has already learned a large correction.
- Clearing codes and learned values before recording trims, which erases the evidence.

## Safety

- Trim testing involves a running engine. Use exhaust extraction indoors, set the parking brake, and keep clear of belts and fans.
- Smoke machines introduce vapor into the intake; follow the tool instructions and keep ignition sources away.
- Have a second person operate the scan tool during road tests.

## Key takeaways

- Positive trim means the module is adding fuel; negative means it is removing fuel.
- Total trim is about STFT plus LTFT; beyond roughly ±10% generally warrants investigation (general guideline — verify against OEM specification).
- Compare trims at idle, 2,500 RPM, and under load; the pattern points to vacuum leaks, fuel delivery, or airflow measurement.
- Compare banks to separate common causes from bank-specific ones.
- Record trims before clearing anything, and confirm closed loop first.

lessons.title: Fuel injector operation and testing
lessons.body:
## How a port fuel injector works

A port fuel injector is an electrically operated valve. Most designs work like this:

- The injector receives **power** from a fused circuit, often through a relay or ignition feed.
- The engine module turns on a **driver transistor that grounds the injector**. Current flows through the coil, the magnetic field lifts the pintle or ball, and fuel sprays.
- The time the injector is held open is the **pulse width**, measured in milliseconds. At a steady fuel pressure, fuel quantity depends on pulse width.
- When the driver turns off, the collapsing magnetic field produces an **inductive voltage spike**, often clamped by the driver circuit.

Most modern port injectors are high-impedance, **saturated-switch** designs. Some older systems used low-impedance injectors with **peak-and-hold** drivers that apply high current to open the injector and then reduce current to hold it open.

## Direct injection injectors

GDI injectors spray into the combustion chamber against high cylinder pressure, so they must open very quickly. The module typically applies a **boosted opening voltage** well above battery voltage, then drops to a lower holding current. Many GDI systems control both the supply and ground sides of each injector. Test them only with the methods in the OEM service information.

## A layered testing approach

Start with fast, non-invasive tests, then move to tests that prove the injector's electrical and mechanical condition.

1. **Scan data:** Review misfire counters, fuel trims by bank, and injector pulse width. A single lean cylinder often shows up as a misfire on that cylinder and positive trims on its bank.
2. **Noid light:** Confirms that a pulse reaches the connector. It does **not** prove the pulse is correct or that the injector flows fuel.
3. **Scope the control side:** A good waveform shows supply voltage, a clean pull toward ground during the pulse, and an inductive spike at turn-off. A weak or missing spike compared with the other injectors can indicate a winding or circuit problem.
4. **Current ramp:** A low-amp current probe shows current building while the injector is energized. A small notch in the ramp, often called the **pintle hump**, shows the moment the injector mechanically opens. Compare injectors on the same engine.
5. **Resistance:** Measure at the same temperature and compare with the OEM specification and with the other injectors.
6. **Balance (pressure drop) test:** Pressurize the rail, energize each injector for the same time with an injector pulser, and record the pressure drop. An injector with a noticeably smaller drop is flowing less; a larger drop indicates more flow. Some procedures state an allowable variation (per OEM specification).
7. **Leakage check:** Low residual pressure, a rich trim at startup, or a wet cylinder can indicate a leaking injector. A badly leaking injector can fill a cylinder with fuel and cause hydrostatic lock.

On port-injected engines, a **swap test** can also help. Move the suspect injector to another cylinder and see whether the fault follows it.

## Worked example (illustrative values)

A four-cylinder engine has a cylinder 2 misfire at idle, with positive fuel trims.

- The misfire stays on cylinder 2 after swapping coils, so the coil is unlikely.
- The spark plug looks similar to the others, and compression is within the general guideline.
- The cylinder 2 injector waveform and current ramp look normal, so the driver and winding are working.
- On a balance test, cylinders 1, 3, and 4 each drop about 9 psi; cylinder 2 drops only 3 psi.

The electrical tests pass but the flow test fails, so the injector is likely **restricted**. Swapping it to another cylinder and seeing the misfire follow, or having it flow-tested, confirms the diagnosis before it is replaced or cleaned.

## Common mistakes

- Treating a noid light flash as proof of a good injector.
- Condemning an injector for a misfire without first checking spark and compression.
- Pulsing injectors on a pressurized rail that is off the engine, which sprays fuel.
- Probing GDI injector circuits with an incandescent test light.

## Safety

- Balance and leakage tests involve pressurized fuel. Relieve pressure per the OEM procedure before opening the system, catch residual fuel, and keep ignition sources away.
- GDI injector circuits operate at elevated voltage and the fuel is under very high pressure. Follow OEM procedures and use appropriate test equipment.
- Running tests require exhaust extraction and clearance from belts and fans.

## Key takeaways

- The module usually grounds a port injector to open it; pulse width controls fuel quantity.
- A noid light proves a pulse exists, not that the injector works.
- Scope voltage and current waveforms test the circuit, winding, and mechanical opening.
- A balance test compares actual flow between injectors.
- Prove the injector is at fault with electrical and flow evidence before replacing it.

quiz.title: Fuel Systems and Fuel Trim Quiz

questions.q: A warm engine in closed loop shows total fuel trim of +22% at idle and +5% at 2,500 RPM with no load. What is the most likely cause?
choices: A weak fuel pump
A vacuum leak
A restricted fuel filter
A leaking fuel injector
questions.explanation: Unmetered air is a large share of total airflow at idle and a small share at higher airflow, so a vacuum leak produces a large correction at idle that shrinks as RPM rises. Fuel delivery faults usually get worse with load, and a leaking injector causes negative (rich) trims.

questions.q: Fuel trims are near 0% at idle but reach about +20% on both banks during a steady loaded cruise. What should you test next?
choices: Smoke test the intake for a vacuum leak
Inspect for an exhaust leak ahead of the bank 1 sensor
Fuel pressure and volume under load
The EVAP purge valve
questions.explanation: A lean condition that appears on both banks and grows with demand points to a common supply problem, such as low fuel pressure or volume, rather than a vacuum leak, which is most visible at idle.

questions.q: Bank 1 total fuel trim is +18% while bank 2 is +2%. Which cause is LEAST likely?
choices: Low fuel pressure
An intake leak at the bank 1 runners
An exhaust leak ahead of the bank 1 upstream sensor
A restricted injector on bank 1
questions.explanation: Fuel pressure is common to both banks, so a pressure problem would normally affect both. A difference between banks points to something specific to the lean bank.

questions.q: Fuel trims are about -15% at idle. When the purge line is disconnected at the intake and capped, trims move toward 0%. What does this indicate?
choices: A vacuum leak at the intake manifold
An EVAP purge valve that is stuck open or leaking
Low fuel pressure
A slow upstream oxygen sensor
questions.explanation: Fuel vapor entering through an unwanted purge flow makes the mixture rich, so the module removes fuel. Blocking the purge path removed the extra vapor, and the trims recovered. Confirm with the OEM purge valve test.

questions.q: What effect does an exhaust leak just ahead of the upstream oxygen sensor typically have on fuel trim?
choices: Negative trim, because the sensor sees extra fuel
No effect, because exhaust leaks only cause noise
The module switches permanently to open loop
Positive trim, because the sensor detects outside oxygen and reports lean
questions.explanation: Exhaust pulses can draw outside air in through the leak. The sensor reads that oxygen as a lean mixture, and the module adds fuel even though the engine was not lean.

questions.q: On a return-type system with a vacuum-referenced regulator, what should fuel pressure do when the vacuum hose is removed from the regulator at idle?
choices: Rise
Drop to zero
Stay exactly the same
Oscillate until the pump shuts off
questions.explanation: Removing manifold vacuum from the regulator makes it behave as it would under load, so rail pressure rises. No change suggests a regulator or reference hose problem, and fuel in the hose indicates a leaking regulator diaphragm.

questions.q: Residual pressure drops quickly after shutdown. With the supply line blocked by a shutoff valve, the rail side holds pressure. Where is the leak?
choices: A leaking injector
The pressure regulator on the rail
The pump check valve or the supply side back toward the tank
The fuel rail pressure sensor
questions.explanation: Blocking the supply isolates the rail. If the rail holds, the injectors and anything else on the rail side are sealing, and the pressure loss is on the pump side, commonly a leaking check valve.

questions.q: A noid light flashes normally at the cylinder 3 injector connector, and cylinder 3 is misfiring. What has the noid light proven?
choices: The injector is good
The injector is restricted
A pulse reaches the connector; the injector's electrical and mechanical condition is still unknown
The engine module is faulty
questions.explanation: A noid light only shows that the driver switches and the circuit carries a pulse. Waveform, current ramp, balance, or swap testing is needed to judge the injector.

questions.q: During an injector balance test, the cylinder 4 injector produces a much larger pressure drop than the others. What does this suggest?
choices: The injector is restricted
The injector flows more fuel than the others, possibly because it is leaking or sticking open
The balance test is invalid on that cylinder
Fuel pump pressure is too low
questions.explanation: Pressure drop reflects how much fuel passed through the injector during the same pulse. A larger drop means more flow, which can make that cylinder run rich.

questions.q: A GDI engine's high-side fuel pressure is below the desired value in scan data. What should you verify first?
choices: Replace the high-pressure pump
Install a mechanical gauge on the high-pressure rail
Replace the rail pressure sensor
The low-pressure supply to the high-pressure pump
questions.explanation: The cam-driven high-pressure pump can only perform if its supply is correct. Check low-side pressure first. Gauges are not installed on the high-pressure side; use scan data and the OEM procedure.

flashcards.back: A pump can hold normal pressure at idle yet fail to supply enough volume at high demand.

flashcards.back: Classic vacuum leak (unmetered air) pattern.

flashcards.back: Suspect fuel delivery: pressure, volume, filter, or restricted injectors.
