courses.title: Ignition Systems
courses.summary: How inductive ignition systems create and time the spark, how coil-on-plug systems are built and tested, how to diagnose misfires with counters, swap tests, and secondary waveforms, and how to read and service spark plugs.

lessons.title: Ignition system fundamentals
lessons.body:
## The job of the ignition system

The ignition system must deliver a spark that is **strong enough** to jump the spark plug gap under compression, **long enough** to ignite the mixture reliably, and **at the right moment** in the cycle. A weakness in any of these three shows up as misfires, poor fuel economy, detonation, or lost power.

## The coil is a transformer

An ignition coil has two windings around a common iron core:

- **Primary winding:** relatively few turns of heavier wire, with low resistance.
- **Secondary winding:** many more turns of very fine wire, with much higher resistance. One end connects to the spark plug.

Because the secondary has far more turns than the primary, a change in magnetic field induces a much higher voltage in the secondary. That turns ratio is how a 12-volt electrical system produces the thousands of volts needed to fire a spark plug.

## Dwell, saturation, and collapse

1. **Dwell (charging):** A driver transistor, in the engine module or in the coil itself, switches on and lets current flow through the primary winding. The magnetic field builds. The time the primary is energized is the dwell time.
2. **Saturation:** After enough dwell time, the field reaches its useful maximum. Too little dwell leaves the coil weak; the module adjusts dwell for battery voltage and engine speed.
3. **Collapse:** The driver switches off. The field collapses rapidly and induces a high voltage in the secondary. Voltage rises until the gas in the plug gap ionizes and current begins to flow as a spark. The primary side also produces an inductive spike of a few hundred volts.

## Required voltage versus available voltage

The voltage needed to start the spark, the **required voltage**, depends on:

- **Plug gap:** wider gaps need more voltage.
- **Cylinder pressure:** higher pressure under load needs more voltage.
- **Mixture:** lean mixtures are harder to ignite and need more voltage.
- **Plug and wire condition:** worn electrodes and high-resistance connections raise the requirement.

The coil's **available voltage** must exceed the required voltage with some reserve. When worn plugs or a weakening coil eat into that reserve, the first symptom is often a **misfire under load**, because that is when required voltage is highest.

## Spark timing

The engine module decides when to fire each coil using the crankshaft and camshaft position sensors, plus inputs such as engine load, engine speed, coolant and intake air temperature, and **knock sensor** feedback.

- Timing **advances** as engine speed rises, because there is less time for the mixture to burn.
- When the knock sensor detects detonation, the module **retards** timing.
- On modern engines, base timing is not adjustable. Scan data shows the timing advance the module is commanding.

## Ignition system types

- **Distributor:** One coil; a rotor and cap route spark to each cylinder. Found on older vehicles.
- **Waste spark:** One coil fires two companion cylinders at once. One cylinder is on compression and uses the spark; the other is on exhaust and wastes it.
- **Coil-on-plug (COP):** One coil sits directly on each spark plug.
- **Coil-near-plug:** One coil per cylinder, connected by a short plug wire.

## Worked example (illustrative values)

Ohm's law shows why modules control dwell and current. If 12 V were applied across a primary winding of 0.6 Ω with nothing limiting current, the current could approach:

- I = E ÷ R = 12 ÷ 0.6 = **20 A**

That would overheat the coil and driver. The module limits dwell, and many drivers limit current, to charge the coil fully without damaging it.

Now consider a vehicle that misfires only when accelerating uphill. Idle is smooth. High load raises cylinder pressure, which raises required voltage. Worn plugs with widened gaps or a weak coil may still fire at idle but run out of reserve under load. The logical tests are checking plug condition and gap, and measuring firing voltage under load, before replacing anything.

## Safety

- Secondary ignition voltage can reach tens of thousands of volts. A shock can cause an involuntary jerk into a fan or belt. People with implanted medical devices should avoid secondary ignition work.
- Never let a coil fire with its output disconnected and no spark tester attached. The spark seeks another path, which can damage the coil or driver and shock the technician.
- The primary side also carries voltage spikes of a few hundred volts.

## Key takeaways

- The coil is a transformer: current flows through the primary during dwell, and field collapse induces high secondary voltage.
- Required voltage rises with gap, cylinder pressure, and lean mixtures; misfires under load often mean the reserve is gone.
- The module sets timing from crank and cam position, load, temperature, and knock feedback.
- Know the system type: distributor, waste spark, coil-on-plug, or coil-near-plug.
- Respect secondary voltage, and never fire a coil into an open circuit.

lessons.title: Coil-on-plug ignition
lessons.body:
## Coil-on-plug construction

In a coil-on-plug (COP) system, each cylinder has its own coil mounted directly on the spark plug. There are no plug wires to leak or fail, each coil has more time to charge between firings, and the module can control each cylinder's timing individually.

A typical COP coil includes:

- The **primary and secondary windings** and iron core in the coil body.
- A **boot and spring** or terminal that connect the secondary output to the spark plug. The boot also seals the plug well against moisture and dirt.
- Often a **high-voltage diode** in the secondary to block the small voltage induced when dwell begins, preventing an early spark.

## Two-wire and multi-wire coils

How the coil is wired tells you how to test it. Always confirm the circuit layout in the wiring diagram for that vehicle.

- **Two-wire coils:** One wire supplies power, usually from an ignition-switched fused circuit. The engine module grounds the primary winding through a **driver transistor inside the module**. The control wire carries the full primary voltage, including the inductive spike.
- **Three- or four-wire coils:** The coil contains its own **igniter (driver)**. It receives power, ground, and a low-voltage **trigger signal** from the module. Some designs add a wire that sends a confirmation signal back to the module or provides a separate ground.

## Common COP failures

- **Cracked or carbon-tracked boots.** High voltage finds an easier path to ground along a damaged boot, especially in wet weather.
- **Internal secondary breakdown** from heat cycling and age.
- **Oil or coolant in the plug well**, often from a leaking valve cover or spark plug tube seal, which attacks the boot.
- **Worn spark plugs.** A worn plug raises the voltage the coil must produce, stressing the coil. A failed coil is often a victim of a neglected plug.
- **Circuit faults:** chafed wiring, poor grounds, corroded connectors, or a failed driver.

## Testing COP systems

1. **Scan data:** Check misfire counters by cylinder and look for coil circuit codes. Generic codes in the P0351–P0362 range identify individual ignition coil circuit faults.
2. **Visual inspection:** Remove the coil and look for carbon tracks (thin lines burned into the boot or coil tower), cracks, swelling, and oil or coolant in the plug well.
3. **Swap test:** Move the suspect coil to a cylinder that is not misfiring and clear the counters. If the misfire moves with the coil, the coil is implicated.
4. **Primary circuit test:** On a two-wire coil, confirm supply voltage and scope the control signal. On a multi-wire coil, confirm power, check the ground with a voltage drop test under load, and scope the trigger signal for a clean pulse.
5. **Secondary test:** A COP probe or capacitive pickup on a scope shows firing voltage and spark duration. An adjustable spark tester proves the coil can fire across a gap that requires high voltage, which is more meaningful than an open-air spark.
6. **Resistance checks:** Useful on some two-wire coils when compared with the OEM specification. Coils with built-in igniters usually cannot be judged by resistance.

## Worked example

A vehicle misfires on cylinder 4, mostly on rainy mornings.

- Misfire counters confirm cylinder 4. No coil circuit code is present.
- The coil boot shows a thin carbon track, and the plug well has engine oil in it.
- The coil is swapped to cylinder 1. On the next damp morning, the misfire moves to cylinder 1, confirming the coil.

Replacing the coil alone would lead to a comeback. The **oil in the plug well** came from a leaking spark plug tube seal, which damaged the boot. The complete repair is the tube seal, the coil, and inspection of the spark plug, followed by verifying that misfire counters stay at zero.

## Safety

- **Do not pull coils off a running engine** to find a dead cylinder. The coil can fire through you or into the engine, damaging the coil or driver. Use misfire counters, a scan tool cylinder contribution test, or an injector disable test instead.
- Keep hands and scope leads away from belts and the cooling fan during running tests.
- Use a proper spark tester rather than holding a plug against the engine.

## Key takeaways

- COP systems use one coil per cylinder; two-wire coils are driven by the engine module, and multi-wire coils contain their own igniter.
- Check the wiring diagram to know which wire carries power, ground, trigger, or feedback.
- Carbon tracking, oil in plug wells, and worn plugs are common reasons coils fail.
- A swap test, circuit test, and secondary test build the evidence before a coil is replaced.
- Fix the root cause, such as a leaking tube seal or a worn plug, not just the failed coil.

lessons.title: Secondary ignition and misfire diagnosis
lessons.body:
## How the module detects a misfire

Every power stroke briefly speeds up the crankshaft. The engine module watches the **crankshaft position sensor** signal, and when a cylinder's power stroke fails to accelerate the crankshaft as expected, it counts a misfire for that cylinder.

- **P0300** indicates a random or multiple-cylinder misfire. **P0301–P0312** identify misfires on specific cylinders.
- A **flashing MIL** indicates misfire severe enough to damage the catalytic converter. The driver should reduce load and have the vehicle serviced promptly.
- A misfire count means the crankshaft slowed down. It does **not** mean the ignition system failed. Fuel, air, and mechanical problems cause misfires too, and rough roads or driveline faults can occasionally mimic them.

## Separate ignition, fuel, and mechanical causes

Start with the evidence the vehicle already gives you:

- **Freeze frame:** RPM, load, coolant temperature, and fuel trim when the misfire set. A misfire only under heavy load suggests low ignition reserve or fuel delivery; a misfire only when cold suggests a different set of causes.
- **Which cylinders:** One cylinder points to parts serving that cylinder, such as its coil, plug, injector, or valves. Random misfires point to something common: a vacuum leak, fuel pressure, cam timing, or a shared power supply.
- **Misfire counters and Mode $06 data:** These show cylinders that are misfiring at low levels, even before a code sets.

For a single cylinder, a logical order is: **swap the coil**, **inspect or swap the spark plug**, **test the injector**, then **test compression**. Each test moves the fault or eliminates a cause.

## Reading a secondary ignition waveform

A scope with a COP probe or capacitive pickup shows what happens inside the spark event. Compare cylinders under the same conditions.

- **Firing line:** The peak voltage needed to ionize the gap and start the spark.
  - **Higher than the other cylinders:** extra resistance, such as a wide plug gap, an open or burned boot connection, or a lean cylinder.
  - **Lower than the other cylinders:** an easier path, such as a fouled plug, a narrow gap, a cracked boot leaking to ground, a rich cylinder, or low compression.
- **Spark line:** The lower, roughly flat voltage while current flows across the gap. Its length is the **burn time**, commonly around 1–2 ms on many systems (general guideline — verify against OEM specification or known-good data).
  - **Short burn time:** Energy was used up on a high firing voltage; suspect high secondary resistance or a lean cylinder.
  - **Long burn time at low voltage:** Suspect a fouled plug or low cylinder pressure.
- **Coil oscillations:** Ringing after the spark ends. Missing oscillations can indicate shorted coil windings.

Snapping the throttle or loading the engine raises cylinder pressure and required voltage, which exposes weak components that look normal at idle.

## Worked example

A vehicle sets **P0302** during highway acceleration. It idles smoothly.

- Freeze frame shows high load and moderate RPM when the code set.
- At idle, all secondary waveforms look similar. On a **snap throttle**, the cylinder 2 firing line rises well above the others and its burn time becomes noticeably shorter.
- Those two changes together point to high resistance in the spark path. The cylinder 2 plug has a badly eroded center electrode, and its gap is far wider than the OEM specification.
- The coil tests normal on a spark tester, so it stays.

The spark plugs are replaced as a set, following the maintenance schedule, and the vehicle is driven under the freeze frame conditions. Misfire counters stay at zero, confirming the repair.

## Common mistakes

- Replacing all coils for a single-cylinder misfire without a swap test.
- Assuming a misfire code means an ignition fault.
- Clearing codes before recording freeze frame data.
- Judging waveforms only at idle, where weak parts often look normal.

## Safety

- Secondary voltage is dangerous. Connect scope probes with the engine off, and route leads away from the fan and belts.
- Misfire testing requires a running engine. Use exhaust extraction indoors and set the parking brake.
- A flashing MIL means catalyst-damaging misfire. Avoid prolonged loaded testing that could overheat the catalytic converter.

## Key takeaways

- The module detects misfires from crankshaft speed changes; the cause can be ignition, fuel, air, or mechanical.
- Use freeze frame, cylinder patterns, and counters to narrow the possibilities before testing.
- Swap tests move the fault and prove which component follows it.
- High firing voltage with short burn time points to resistance; low firing voltage with long burn time points to an easy path or low cylinder pressure.
- Verify the repair under the conditions that caused the misfire.

lessons.title: Reading and servicing spark plugs
lessons.body:
## Spark plug construction

A spark plug looks simple, but each part has a job:

- **Terminal:** Connects to the coil boot or plug wire.
- **Ceramic insulator:** Keeps high voltage from escaping to the shell and conducts heat away from the tip.
- **Built-in resistor:** Reduces radio-frequency interference that can disrupt electronics.
- **Shell and seat:** The threads and either a **gasket seat** or a **tapered seat** seal the plug in the cylinder head and transfer heat to it.
- **Center and ground electrodes:** Form the gap the spark must jump.

## Heat range

Heat range describes how quickly a plug moves heat from its insulator tip into the cylinder head.

- A **hotter** plug has a longer insulator path, so the tip runs hotter and burns off deposits more readily.
- A **colder** plug transfers heat faster and resists overheating.

A plug that runs too cold can foul; one that runs too hot can overheat and cause pre-ignition. Always use the plug type and heat range specified in the OEM service information.

## Electrode materials and gap

- **Copper-core nickel** plugs are inexpensive but wear faster.
- **Platinum and iridium** plugs use fine, hard electrodes that resist wear and need less voltage to fire. Many are designed for long replacement intervals, as listed in the OEM maintenance schedule.
- Check the gap with a **wire-type gauge** against the OEM specification. Never pry against the center electrode of a fine-wire plug; bend only the ground electrode if adjustment is allowed. A dropped plug may have a cracked insulator or a changed gap.

## Reading spark plugs

Remove the plugs in order and keep them labeled by cylinder. **Compare them to each other.** One plug that looks different from the rest points to a problem in that cylinder.

- **Normal:** Light tan to gray insulator, little deposit, and even electrode wear.
- **Carbon fouled:** Dry, black, sooty deposits. Suspect a rich mixture, weak spark, extended idling, or a plug running too cold.
- **Oil fouled:** Wet, oily black deposits. Oil is entering the chamber past the rings, valve guides or seals, through a PCV fault, or from a turbocharger seal.
- **Wet with fuel:** The cylinder is not firing, or it is flooding, possibly from a leaking injector.
- **Unusually clean or white deposits on one plug:** Can indicate coolant entering the cylinder. Confirm with a cooling system pressure test or combustion leak test.
- **Overheated:** Blistered white insulator and eroded electrodes. Suspect a lean mixture, excessive timing advance, a cooling problem, or the wrong heat range.
- **Cracked insulator tip:** Often caused by detonation, or by mishandling during installation.
- **Melted electrodes:** Pre-ignition damage. Find the cause before the engine is damaged.
- **Crusty ash deposits:** Burned oil or fuel additives.

## Removal and installation

1. Let the engine cool. Removing plugs from a hot engine increases the risk of damaging aluminum cylinder head threads.
2. **Blow debris out of the plug wells** before removal, so dirt does not fall into the cylinder.
3. Start new plugs **by hand** to prevent cross-threading.
4. Tighten to the torque value in the OEM or spark plug manufacturer's specification. Gasket-seat and tapered-seat plugs are tightened differently.
5. Use anti-seize only if the plug manufacturer recommends it. Many plated plugs do not require it, and anti-seize changes the effective torque.
6. Reinstall coils fully seated, with boots in good condition.

## Worked example

A V6 has a cylinder 5 misfire. All plugs look normal except cylinder 5, which is **wet with oily black deposits**. A new plug would stop the misfire briefly, then foul again.

The plug is evidence, not the cause. The next step is to find how oil is reaching cylinder 5: a compression test with a wet test, then a cylinder leakage test to check ring sealing. If sealing is good, valve guides or seals become the prime suspect. The repair addresses the oil source, and the plug is replaced as part of that repair.

## Safety

- Exhaust manifolds and turbochargers sit near spark plugs on many engines and stay hot long after shutdown. Let the engine cool.
- Wear eye protection when blowing out plug wells.
- Disable ignition per the service information before cranking with plugs removed, and make sure every coil is reconnected before starting.

## Key takeaways

- Use the OEM-specified plug type, heat range, and gap.
- Compare plugs between cylinders; the odd one out identifies the problem cylinder.
- Plug appearance points to causes such as rich running, oil entry, coolant entry, overheating, or detonation, which you then confirm by testing.
- Remove plugs from a cool engine, start them by hand, and torque to the published specification.
- A fouled plug is usually a symptom; find and fix what fouled it.

questions.q: An engine idles smoothly but misfires during hard acceleration. Why does ignition weakness often show up only under load?
choices: Timing is always retarded at idle
Injectors close fully at high RPM
The crankshaft sensor only reports at idle
Higher cylinder pressure under load raises the voltage required to fire, exposing worn plugs or a weak coil
questions.explanation: Required voltage rises with cylinder pressure, plug gap, and lean mixtures. A marginal plug or coil can fire at idle but run out of reserve under load.

questions.q: A cylinder 3 misfire moves to cylinder 1 after the coils on those two cylinders are swapped. What is implicated?
choices: The ignition coil
The cylinder 3 spark plug
The cylinder 3 injector
Low compression in cylinder 3
questions.explanation: The only thing that moved was the coil, and the misfire followed it. Plugs, injectors, and compression stayed with cylinder 3.

questions.q: On a secondary waveform, one cylinder shows a much higher firing line and a shorter burn time than the others. What does this suggest?
choices: A fouled spark plug
A rich mixture in that cylinder
Excess resistance in the spark path, such as a wide plug gap or a poor boot connection
Low compression in that cylinder
questions.explanation: More resistance requires more voltage to start the spark, which uses more of the coil's energy and leaves less for burn time. Fouled plugs, rich mixtures, and low compression tend to lower firing voltage instead.

questions.q: One cylinder shows a low firing line and a long, low spark line compared with the other cylinders. What is a likely cause?
choices: A wide spark plug gap
A fouled plug or low cylinder pressure
A lean mixture in that cylinder
An open circuit in the coil boot
questions.explanation: An easy path, such as a fouled plug, or lower cylinder pressure reduces the voltage needed to start and sustain the spark. Wide gaps, lean mixtures, and open circuits raise firing voltage.

questions.q: On a two-wire coil-on-plug system, what switches the coil's primary circuit?
choices: An igniter inside the coil
The ignition switch
A relay in the underhood fuse box
A driver transistor inside the engine module
questions.explanation: Two-wire coils receive power on one wire, and the engine module grounds the other through its internal driver. Multi-wire coils contain their own igniter and receive a low-voltage trigger signal.

questions.q: A vehicle has P0300 with misfire counts spread across several cylinders. What is the best initial direction?
choices: Replace all ignition coils
Look for a cause common to all cylinders, such as a vacuum leak, fuel pressure, cam timing, or a shared coil power supply
Replace the cylinder 1 spark plug
Replace the crankshaft position sensor
questions.explanation: Random misfires usually come from something every cylinder shares. Test the common factors before replacing parts on individual cylinders.

questions.q: A coil boot is carbon-tracked, and the plug well contains engine oil. What is the complete repair?
choices: Repair the leaking tube or valve cover seal, replace the damaged coil or boot, and inspect the plug
Replace the coil only
Wipe out the oil and reinstall the coil
Replace all the spark plugs only
questions.explanation: The oil caused the boot damage. Replacing only the coil leaves the root cause in place and leads to a comeback.

questions.q: One spark plug is wet with oily black deposits while the others look normal. What is the best next step?
choices: Install a hotter heat range plug in that cylinder
Replace that cylinder's fuel injector
Test ring and valve sealing on that cylinder with compression and leakage tests
Replace that cylinder's coil
questions.explanation: Oil fouling means oil is reaching the chamber. Compression, wet, and leakage testing identify whether rings, valve guides or seals, or another source is responsible.

questions.q: Why shouldn't you pull coils off a running engine to find the dead cylinder?
choices: It resets the fuel trims
The coil can fire through you or another path, risking shock and damage to the coil or driver
The engine will not restart afterward
It erases the misfire counters
questions.explanation: Secondary voltage seeks a path to ground. Use misfire counters, a cylinder contribution test, or an injector disable test instead.

questions.q: What is the main risk of installing a spark plug with a hotter heat range than the OEM specifies?
choices: Increased carbon fouling
Lower firing voltage with no drawbacks
Tip overheating that can lead to pre-ignition and engine damage
A shorter spark duration only
questions.explanation: A hotter plug holds more heat at its tip. Under high load, the tip can become hot enough to ignite the mixture before the spark, a condition that can damage pistons. Use the OEM-specified plug.

flashcards.back: Relatively few turns of heavier wire; current flows through it during dwell to build the magnetic field.
Many turns of fine wire; field collapse induces the high voltage that fires the spark plug.
The time the primary circuit is energized to charge the coil.

flashcards.front: What happens when the driver switches off?
flashcards.back: The magnetic field collapses and induces high voltage in the secondary until the plug gap fires.
Wider plug gaps, higher cylinder pressure, lean mixtures, and worn or high-resistance components.
One coil fires two companion cylinders at once: one on compression and one on exhaust.
Power on one wire; the engine module's driver grounds the other to switch the primary.
Contains its own igniter; receives power, ground, and a low-voltage trigger, sometimes with a feedback wire.
Thin burned paths on a boot or coil tower where high voltage leaks to ground, often worse when damp.
Random or multiple-cylinder misfire detected.
Misfire severe enough to damage the catalytic converter.

flashcards.front: How does the module detect misfire?
flashcards.back: By watching for crankshaft speed dropping on a cylinder's power stroke.
The peak secondary voltage needed to ionize the plug gap and start the spark.
Spark duration, commonly around 1–2 ms on many systems (general guideline — verify against OEM specification or known-good data).

flashcards.front: High firing line with short burn time
flashcards.back: Excess resistance in the spark path, such as a wide gap or poor connection, or a lean cylinder.
How quickly the plug transfers heat from its tip to the cylinder head; hotter plugs retain more heat.
Dry black soot; suspect a rich mixture, weak spark, extended idling, or a plug running too cold.

flashcards.front: Why remove spark plugs from a cool engine?
flashcards.back: To reduce the risk of damaging threads in aluminum cylinder heads.

courses.title: Automotive Electrical Fundamentals
courses.summary: Ohm's law applied to real vehicle circuits, voltage drop testing, reading wiring diagrams, relays and circuit protection, and testing batteries, starting, and charging systems.

lessons.title: Ohm's law applied to vehicle circuits
lessons.body:
## Three quantities, one relationship

Every electrical diagnosis comes back to three quantities:

- **Voltage (E), in volts:** electrical pressure, the push that moves current.
- **Current (I), in amps:** the flow of electrons through the circuit.
- **Resistance (R), in ohms:** opposition to current flow.

**Ohm's law** ties them together: **E = I × R**. Rearranged, **I = E ÷ R** and **R = E ÷ I**. The Ohm's law triangle is a memory aid: cover the quantity you want, and the other two show how to calculate it.

**Power (P), in watts**, is the rate at which a circuit does work or makes heat: **P = E × I**. Because E = I × R, power can also be written as P = I² × R, which explains why a small resistance carrying a large current gets very hot.

## Series circuits

In a series circuit there is only one path for current.

- The **same current** flows through every part.
- **Total resistance** is the sum of all resistances.
- The **voltage drops** across all parts add up to the source voltage.

That last rule is the key to diagnosis: an unwanted resistance in series with a load takes voltage away from the load.

## Parallel circuits

In a parallel circuit, current divides among branches.

- Each branch receives the **same voltage**.
- **Branch currents add** to make the total current.
- **Total resistance is lower than the smallest branch.** For two equal branches it is half of one branch. The general formula is 1 ÷ Rtotal = 1 ÷ R1 + 1 ÷ R2 + ...

Most vehicle circuits are **series-parallel**: several loads in parallel share a fuse, a feed wire, and a ground path that are in series with all of them.

## Three fault types in Ohm's law terms

- **Open circuit:** Resistance is effectively infinite, so current is zero. The load does not work, and no fuse blows.
- **High resistance:** An unwanted series resistance, such as corrosion or a loose terminal, reduces current and steals voltage from the load. The load works poorly.
- **Short to ground:** Current bypasses the load through a low-resistance path. Resistance drops, current rises sharply, and the fuse should open.

## Worked example 1: a corroded ground (illustrative values)

A lamp with a resistance of 2 Ω is powered by 12 V.

- Normal: I = 12 ÷ 2 = **6 A**, and P = 12 × 6 = **72 W**.

Corrosion adds 0.5 Ω at the ground connection:

- Total R = 2 + 0.5 = 2.5 Ω, so I = 12 ÷ 2.5 = **4.8 A**
- Voltage across the lamp = 4.8 × 2 = **9.6 V**
- Voltage across the corrosion = 4.8 × 0.5 = **2.4 V**
- Lamp power = 9.6 × 4.8 ≈ **46 W**, so the lamp is visibly dim
- Heat at the corrosion = 2.4 × 4.8 ≈ **11.5 W**, concentrated in one small connection

That heat is why high-resistance connections discolor, melt connectors, and get worse over time. Notice that the 2.4 V lost at the connection would appear on a voltmeter as a **voltage drop**, the subject of the next lesson.

## Worked example 2: parallel loads (illustrative values)

Two 2 Ω lamps are connected in parallel to 12 V.

- Each branch: I = 12 ÷ 2 = **6 A**
- Total current: 6 + 6 = **12 A**
- Total resistance: 12 V ÷ 12 A = **1 Ω**, half of one branch

If one lamp burns out, its branch opens. The other lamp still receives 12 V and draws 6 A, and total current falls to 6 A. This is why one failed bulb does not usually disable the other lamps on the same circuit.

## Using Ohm's law in diagnosis

Ohm's law lets you **predict** what a healthy circuit should do and compare it with what you measure:

- Lower-than-expected current with full supply voltage suggests added resistance.
- Current far above normal suggests a short or a mechanically binding motor.
- A load that receives low voltage while the battery is healthy means voltage is being lost somewhere in series with it.

Reason from the numbers before reaching for parts.

## Safety

- A short circuit has very low resistance, so current can reach hundreds of amps directly at the battery. A wrench across the positive terminal and ground can weld, burn, and cause the battery to fail violently.
- Fuses are sized to protect the wiring. Never install a larger fuse than specified; the wire becomes the fuse.

## Key takeaways

- E = I × R and P = E × I underpin every electrical test you perform.
- Series circuits share current and divide voltage; parallel circuits share voltage and divide current.
- High resistance in series with a load steals voltage from the load and creates heat at the fault.
- Opens stop current, shorts increase it, and high resistance reduces it.
- Predict expected values with Ohm's law, then measure and compare.

lessons.title: Voltage drop testing
lessons.body:
## What voltage drop is

When current flows through any part of a circuit, some voltage is used up, or dropped, across that part. In a healthy circuit:

- The **load** (a motor, lamp, or solenoid) drops nearly all of the source voltage, because that is where the work is done.
- **Wires, connections, switches, and grounds** drop very little.

A voltage drop test measures how much voltage is lost across a section of the circuit **while it carries its normal operating current**. Excessive drop across something that should only conduct means unwanted resistance.

## Why voltage drop beats an ohmmeter

- It tests the circuit **under real load current**. A wire with only a few strands left can read nearly 0 Ω on an ohmmeter, which uses a tiny test current, yet drop several volts when it carries 10 A.
- It usually does **not require disconnecting anything**, so you do not disturb an intermittent connection before you measure it.
- It tests the **whole path at once**, then lets you narrow it down.

## The one rule you cannot skip

**The circuit must be on and carrying current.** With no current flow there is no voltage drop, even across a badly corroded connection. Operate the load, crank the engine, or turn on the lamp while you measure.

## How to measure

Set the DMM to DC volts and connect it **across** the section being tested:

- **Power side:** Red lead on the battery positive **post**, black lead on the load's power terminal.
- **Ground side:** Red lead on the load's ground terminal, black lead on the battery negative **post**.
- **A single component:** Leads on each side of the switch, connector, relay contact, or fuse.

Place the leads on the battery posts themselves, not the cable clamps, so a bad post-to-clamp connection is included in the test.

## How much drop is too much?

Compare with the OEM specification when one is published. As a general guideline, a single connection should drop no more than about 0.1 V, and the entire power or ground side of a typical circuit no more than a few tenths of a volt. High-current circuits such as starter cables are commonly allowed up to about 0.5 V (general guideline — verify against OEM specification). Low-current sensor circuits should show far less, often only a few millivolts.

## Narrowing it down

When one side of a circuit shows excessive drop, **move the leads inward** to split that side into sections: battery post to clamp, cable to the next connection, connector to connector. The section that shows the drop contains the fault. Each measurement cuts the search area.

## Worked example: slow cranking (illustrative values)

The engine cranks slowly. The battery is fully charged and passes a battery test, so the next step is voltage drop testing while cranking, with fuel or ignition disabled per the service information.

- **Positive side**, battery positive post to the starter's battery terminal: **1.2 V**. Far above the general guideline.
- **Ground side**, starter housing or engine block to the battery negative post: **0.2 V**. Acceptable.

The positive side contains the problem. Splitting it:

- Battery positive post to the positive cable clamp: **0.9 V**.

Most of the loss is at one connection. The clamp is corroded on the inside and loose on the post. After cleaning and tightening, the positive side drops **0.2 V**, cranking speed is normal, and no starter or cable was replaced.

## Where voltage drop testing shines

- Slow cranking and starter clicks
- Undercharging with a healthy alternator
- Dim lamps and slow motors, such as blowers, windows, and fuel pumps
- Intermittent sensor readings caused by shared grounds
- Hot or discolored connectors

## Safety

- Cranking tests produce hundreds of amps. Keep test leads, hands, and tools away from the fan, belts, and pulleys, and route leads so they cannot be caught.
- Disable fuel or ignition per the service information so the engine does not start during cranking tests.
- Use insulated probes and remove jewelry around battery and starter terminals.

## Key takeaways

- Voltage drop testing finds unwanted resistance under real operating current.
- The circuit must be carrying current, or the test will miss the fault.
- Test the power side and the ground side separately, then split the failing side into sections.
- Compare readings with OEM specifications or clearly labeled general guidelines.
- Measure at battery posts, not clamps, so the post connection is included.

lessons.title: Wiring diagrams, relays, and circuit protection
lessons.body:
## Reading a wiring diagram

A wiring diagram is a map of how current flows, not a picture of where wires are routed. Most OEM diagrams place power sources near the top and grounds near the bottom, so current generally flows down the page. Learn the common symbols:

- **Battery, ground,** and **fuse** or **fusible link**
- **Switch:** normally open or normally closed
- **Relay:** a coil drawn next to the contacts it operates
- **Loads:** motors, lamps, solenoids, and resistors
- **Splice:** a dot where wires join
- **Connector:** a break in the wire labeled with a connector ID and **cavity number**
- **Ground point:** a ground symbol with a location ID, found in the ground distribution or component location pages

Diagrams also note **when a circuit is powered**, such as hot at all times, hot in run, or hot in accessory. Wire colors are abbreviated; check the legend in the service information.

## Tracing a circuit

1. Find the **load** that does not work.
2. Trace **power backward** through connectors, switches, and relays to its fuse and source.
3. Trace **ground forward** to its ground point.
4. Note everything that **shares** that fuse, splice, or ground.

Shared components are powerful clues. If two unrelated items fail together, look at the diagram for what they have in common.

When you probe a connector, confirm whether the diagram shows the **terminal side** or the **wire side** view, so you do not test the wrong cavity.

## Relays

A relay lets a small current control a large one. A low-current **control circuit** energizes the relay coil, and its magnetic field closes **contacts** that switch the high-current **load circuit**.

On many ISO mini relays, the terminals are numbered:

- **85 and 86:** coil
- **30:** common input to the contacts
- **87:** normally open output
- **87a:** normally closed output, on five-pin relays

Always confirm terminal use with the wiring diagram for that vehicle. The coil can be switched on its ground side by a module or on its power side by a switch.

**Testing a relay circuit:**

- Confirm the **control side**: coil power, and ground or command, when the relay should be on.
- Confirm the **load side**: voltage in at terminal 30 and out at 87 with the load operating.
- Check **voltage drop across the contacts** under load. A relay can click loudly and still have burned contacts that cannot carry current.
- Substituting a known-good relay with the **same part number** is a quick check, but still confirm the circuit.

## Circuit protection

Protection devices open a circuit when current exceeds a safe level, protecting the **wiring**.

- **Fuses:** A metal strip melts on overcurrent. Blade, cartridge, and high-current styles are common.
- **Fusible links:** Short sections of special wire or high-current fuses near the battery that protect main feeds.
- **Circuit breakers:** Bimetal devices that open when hot; some reset automatically, others manually.
- **PTC devices:** Solid-state devices whose resistance rises sharply when overheated and returns to normal after they cool. They are often built into motors and modules.

## Diagnosing a blown fuse

A fuse is a messenger. It opened because current was too high, usually because of a **short to ground**.

- Do not keep installing fuses to find the short.
- Use the diagram to list every load and branch on that fuse.
- Temporarily replace the fuse with a **fused test device, circuit breaker tester, or short-finding tool**, so the circuit stays protected while you search.
- Unplug loads and harness sections one at a time until the short disappears.
- Inspect wiring where it passes brackets, body openings, seat tracks, and door hinges.

## Worked example

The dome light and the power mirrors both stopped working. The diagram shows they share one fuse, and that fuse is open.

- A circuit breaker tester is installed in the fuse cavity. It trips immediately.
- Unplugging the mirror switch does not change it. Unplugging the dome light connector stops the tripping.
- The dome light feed is traced to the headliner, where the wire has chafed through against a metal bracket.

The wire is repaired and protected, a correct-rating fuse is installed, and both circuits work. Replacing only the fuse would have led to another failure.

## Safety

- **Never bypass a fuse** with wire or install a higher-rated fuse. The wiring becomes the fuse and can burn.
- Use only fused jumper wires when you energize a circuit for testing.
- Disconnect the battery per the OEM procedure before repairing wiring near main feeds.

## Key takeaways

- Trace power back to the source and ground forward to the ground point, and note shared components.
- A relay has a control side and a load side; test both, and check voltage drop across the contacts.
- Fuses protect wiring; a blown fuse means something drew too much current.
- Find shorts with a protected test device and systematic unplugging, not repeated fuses.
- Confirm terminal numbering and connector views in the wiring diagram for the specific vehicle.

lessons.title: Batteries, starting, and charging systems
lessons.body:
## The battery

A 12-volt lead-acid battery has six cells connected in series. Common types include **flooded**, **enhanced flooded (EFB)**, and **absorbed glass mat (AGM)**. Start-stop vehicles usually require EFB or AGM. Replace a battery with the type and rating specified by the OEM; many vehicles also require **battery registration** with a scan tool so the charging strategy matches the new battery.

**State of charge** can be estimated from open-circuit voltage once surface charge has dissipated. As a general guideline for a flooded battery at room temperature, about 12.6 V or higher is fully charged, about 12.4 V is roughly 75%, and about 12.2 V is roughly 50% (general guideline — verify against the battery manufacturer's specification). Charge a low battery before testing it.

**Battery testing:**

- **Conductance testers** estimate battery health; enter the correct battery type and rating.
- A **load test** applies a heavy load for a short time. A traditional guideline is that voltage should stay above about 9.6 V during the test at room temperature (general guideline — verify against the tester and battery manufacturer).

## The starting system

The starting system has two circuits:

- **Control circuit:** The ignition switch or start button signals a module or starter relay, often through a transmission range or clutch switch, to energize the starter solenoid.
- **High-current circuit:** The battery cables and solenoid contacts carry the heavy current the starter motor needs.

Diagnosis follows the symptoms:

- **No crank, no click:** Check battery state, the control circuit, and inputs such as the range switch.
- **Click but no crank:** Check voltage drop in the high-current circuit and battery condition before condemning the starter.
- **Slow crank:** Check battery state of charge, cable voltage drops, starter current draw against the OEM specification, and engine mechanical drag.

## The charging system

The alternator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.

- The **rotor** creates a magnetic field, controlled by the voltage regulator.
- The **stator** produces alternating current.
- **Rectifier diodes** convert it to direct current.
- The **voltage regulator** controls output. On many modern vehicles, the engine module or a body module commands charging voltage based on battery temperature, state of charge, and electrical load.

Conventional systems often charge around 13.5–14.8 V (general guideline — smart charging systems vary widely; verify against OEM specification).

**Testing an undercharging complaint:**

1. Confirm the battery is charged and healthy.
2. Inspect the drive belt and connections.
3. Measure **voltage drop** on the alternator output cable and alternator ground while the alternator is loaded.
4. Perform an **output test** under load and compare with the OEM rating.
5. Check **AC ripple** on the output. Excessive ripple indicates a failed diode or stator winding.
6. On smart charging systems, check commanded versus actual charging in scan data before condemning the alternator.

## Parasitic draw

A small key-off current keeps memory and modules alive. Excessive draw drains the battery while the vehicle sits.

- Measure with a low-amp clamp or with a DMM in series, using a **shunt switch** so opening the circuit does not wake modules.
- Close the doors or latches and wait for modules to go to sleep, which can take a significant time.
- Many vehicles settle below about 50 mA after sleep (general guideline — verify against OEM specification).
- Find the circuit by measuring the **small voltage drop across each fuse** with a DMM. This avoids pulling fuses and waking modules.

## Worked example (illustrative values)

A vehicle's battery is dead after sitting for three days. After charging, the battery passes a conductance test.

- After the modules sleep, key-off draw is **350 mA**, far above the general guideline.
- Measuring the millivolt drop across each fuse shows current flowing only through the fuse for the interior lamps.
- The glove box lamp is on because its switch is damaged.

Repairing the switch drops the draw back into the normal range. A new battery would have been drained the same way.

## Safety

- Batteries release **hydrogen gas**. Avoid sparks and flames; make the final jumper or charger connection per the OEM procedure, typically away from the battery.
- Starter and alternator cables carry very high current. Disconnect the battery per the OEM procedure before servicing them.
- Keep hands and leads away from the drive belt and fan during charging tests.

## Key takeaways

- Charge and test the battery first; many starting and charging complaints begin there.
- Separate starter problems into control-circuit and high-current-circuit faults.
- Test charging systems with voltage drop, output, and ripple checks, and check smart charging commands.
- Measure parasitic draw after modules sleep, and locate it with voltage drop across fuses.
- Follow OEM procedures for battery type, registration, and jump-starting.

questions.q: A headlamp is dim. With the lamp on, you measure 2.4 V between the lamp's ground terminal and the battery negative post. What does this indicate?
choices: A weak bulb filament
A discharged battery
High resistance in the ground path
An open headlamp switch
questions.explanation: The ground path should drop only a small fraction of a volt. A 2.4 V drop means unwanted resistance in the ground path is stealing voltage from the lamp. An open switch would stop current entirely.

questions.q: A technician measures 0 V across a visibly corroded connector with the circuit switched off. Why doesn't this prove the connector is good?
choices: No current is flowing, so there is no voltage drop even across a bad connection
Corrosion has no electrical resistance
Voltage drop must be measured on the AC scale
The battery is too weak to show a reading
questions.explanation: Voltage drop equals current times resistance. With zero current, the drop is zero regardless of resistance. Operate the circuit and measure again.

questions.q: A 12 V source powers a 3 Ω resistance and a 1 Ω resistance in series. What are the circuit current and the voltage across the 1 Ω resistance?
choices: 4 A and 4 V
12 A and 3 V
3 A and 9 V
3 A and 3 V
questions.explanation: Total resistance is 4 Ω, so I = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 A. The drop across the 1 Ω resistance is 3 A × 1 Ω = 3 V; the other 9 V drops across the 3 Ω resistance.

questions.q: Two 6 Ω loads are connected in parallel across 12 V. What is the total current?
choices: 2 A
4 A
1 A
8 A
questions.explanation: Each branch receives the full 12 V and draws 12 ÷ 6 = 2 A. Branch currents add, so the total is 4 A, which corresponds to a total resistance of 3 Ω.

questions.q: A fuse blows immediately every time it is replaced. What is the best approach?
choices: Install a higher-rated fuse
Replace the circuit's relay
Install a fused test device or circuit breaker tester in the fuse cavity and unplug loads one at a time
Keep installing new fuses while wiggling the harness
questions.explanation: A protected test device keeps the circuit safe while you isolate the short by unplugging loads and harness sections. A larger fuse risks burning the wiring.

questions.q: A relay clicks when commanded, but the load does not run. With the relay energized, terminal 30 has battery voltage and terminal 87 has 0 V. What is the likely fault?
choices: An open relay coil
The relay contacts are not closing or are burned
The load is shorted to ground
The module is not commanding the relay
questions.explanation: The click shows the coil is energized, so the control side works. Power is present at the contact input but not at the output, so the contacts are not passing current.

questions.q: During cranking, the starter positive side shows a 1.2 V drop and the ground side shows 0.1 V. What is the next step?
choices: Split the positive side into sections to find the connection or cable causing the drop
Replace the starter
Replace the battery
Clean the engine ground connection
questions.explanation: The ground side is acceptable, and the positive side has excessive drop. Moving the leads inward, from the battery post to the clamp and along the cable, pinpoints the faulty section.

questions.q: Why is a shunt switch or a low-amp clamp preferred over simply disconnecting a battery cable to insert a meter for a parasitic draw test?
choices: Meters cannot measure DC current
It prevents the battery from discharging during the test
Clamps are more accurate than any DMM
Opening the circuit can wake modules and restart their sleep timers, producing a falsely high reading
questions.explanation: Breaking battery power resets or wakes many modules. A shunt switch or clamp keeps the circuit intact, so modules can go to sleep and the true key-off draw can be measured.

questions.q: On a vehicle with smart charging, you see about 12.9 V at steady cruise with a fully charged battery. What should you do?
choices: Replace the alternator
Replace the battery
Check commanded charging in scan data and the OEM charging strategy before condemning parts
Install a higher-output alternator
questions.explanation: Smart charging systems often lower charging voltage when the battery is full to save fuel. Compare the command with the actual output and the OEM description before deciding there is a fault.

questions.q: A 60 W load operates on a 12 V circuit. How much current does it draw?
choices: 5 A
questions.explanation: P = E × I, so I = P ÷ E = 60 ÷ 12 = 5 A. Knowing expected current helps you judge whether a measured draw is normal.

flashcards.back: E = I × R (volts = amps × ohms). Rearranged: I = E ÷ R, R = E ÷ I.
P = E × I (watts). Also P = I² × R.
Same current everywhere; resistances add; voltage drops add up to source voltage.
Same voltage across each branch; branch currents add; total resistance is less than the smallest branch.
Effectively infinite resistance, no current; the load does not work and no fuse blows.
A low-resistance path that bypasses the load; current rises and the fuse should open.

flashcards.front: Effect of high resistance in series with a load
flashcards.back: Reduces current, steals voltage from the load, and creates heat at the fault.
The circuit must be on and carrying its normal current.

flashcards.front: Voltage drop guideline for a single connection
flashcards.back: About 0.1 V or less (general guideline — verify against OEM specification).

flashcards.front: Why voltage drop beats an ohmmeter
flashcards.back: It tests the circuit under real load current, finding faults a tiny ohmmeter test current can pass through.
The relay coil (control side). Confirm in the wiring diagram.
30 = common input; 87 = normally open output; 87a = normally closed output. Confirm in the wiring diagram.
The wiring. Never install a higher rating than specified.
A solid-state protector whose resistance rises sharply when overheated and resets after cooling.

flashcards.front: Open-circuit voltage of a fully charged flooded battery
flashcards.back: About 12.6 V or higher (general guideline — verify against the battery manufacturer's specification).
Excessive ripple on the output points to a failed rectifier diode or stator winding.

flashcards.front: Parasitic draw guideline after modules sleep
flashcards.back: Many vehicles settle below about 50 mA (general guideline — verify against OEM specification).

flashcards.front: Non-invasive way to find a parasitic draw circuit
flashcards.back: Measure the millivolt drop across each fuse; a drop shows current is flowing through that fuse.

courses.title: Diagnostic Strategy and Scan Data
courses.summary: Strategy-based diagnostics for efficient, provable repairs: using scan data and freeze frame, reading Mode $06 test results, and balancing known pattern failures against confirming tests.

lessons.title: Strategy-based diagnostics
lessons.body:
## From process to strategy

The basic diagnostic process tells you what steps to follow. **Strategy** tells you which test to perform next. An experienced technician is not faster because of guessing well; they choose tests that eliminate the most possibilities for the least time and effort, and they let each result change the plan.

## 1. Define the fault precisely

A clear fault definition limits the possibilities before any test.

- **Type:** no-start, driveability, noise, electrical function, or warning lamp only.
- **Behavior:** hard fault that is present now, or intermittent.
- **Conditions:** temperature, load, speed, weather, time since start.

"Stalls when coming to a stop after the engine is fully warm" points to a different set of causes than "stalls randomly."

## 2. Understand how the system works

Read the **description and operation** and the **conditions for setting** the code. Then ask: *how could this system produce this exact symptom?* A module can only set a code based on what it measures, so know which inputs it uses and what it compares them against.

## 3. Build and rank the candidate list

List causes that can explain **all** of the evidence. Rank them by:

- **Likelihood:** known patterns, age and mileage, conditions, and recent repairs.
- **Test cost:** time, access, and risk of disturbing the fault.

A cause that is likely and cheap to test goes first. A likely cause that is expensive to test may still wait until a cheap test has narrowed the field.

## 4. Choose tests that split the possibilities

The most valuable test divides the remaining causes into groups and tells you which group contains the fault.

- In a circuit, test at a **midpoint connector** to learn whether the fault is upstream or downstream.
- In an engine, determine whether the problem is **air, fuel, spark, compression, or timing** before examining parts.
- Start with **zero-disassembly evidence**: scan data, freeze frame, DTC status, and Mode $06.

A useful check before any test: *would a different result change my next step?* If every possible result leads to the same action, the test can wait.

## 5. Update after every result

Each result raises some possibilities and lowers others. Write results down, including normal ones. Watch for **confirmation bias**, which is the tendency to explain away results that do not fit your favorite theory. If the evidence contradicts your theory, change the theory.

## 6. Prove it, repair it, and verify it

Stop testing when you have **direct evidence** of the cause, such as a measurement that fails the specification in a way that explains the symptom. After the repair, repeat the test that failed and confirm that it now passes, then verify under the original conditions.

## Worked example: crank, no start

A warm engine cranks normally but will not start. The candidates include fuel, spark, compression or timing, the immobilizer, and crankshaft signal problems.

1. **Scan data first:** Engine RPM displays during cranking, so the crank signal reaches the module. The immobilizer status is normal, and fuel rail pressure reaches the desired value. Three groups are eliminated without tools.
2. **Spark:** A spark tester on one coil shows strong spark while cranking.
3. **Fuel delivery to the cylinders:** A noid light shows injector pulses.
4. **Mechanical:** A relative compression test shows even current peaks, but they are **unusually low on every cylinder**, and cranking sounds faster than normal.

Every cylinder is weak at once, with spark and fuel present. The common factor is **cam timing**. A cam/crank signal comparison on a scope, followed by an inspection of the timing marks, confirms that the timing chain has jumped. Coils, injectors, and the fuel pump were never suspected long enough to be replaced.

## Common strategy errors

- Starting with the most expensive or invasive test.
- Chasing the code description instead of the system that produces it.
- Testing only what you expect to fail, without confirming what works.
- Clearing codes or disconnecting the battery before recording data.

## Safety

- Crank-no-start testing can flood a cylinder or cause backfires. Follow the service information for disabling fuel or ignition during each test.
- Keep test leads away from belts and fans during cranking and running tests.
- Run engines indoors only with exhaust extraction.

## Key takeaways

- Define the fault precisely, including its conditions.
- Understand how the system sets the code before testing parts.
- Rank causes by likelihood and test cost, and choose tests that split the possibilities.
- Use scan data and other zero-disassembly evidence first.
- Update your thinking after each result, prove the cause directly, and verify the repair.

lessons.title: Scan data and freeze frame
lessons.body:
## Generic and enhanced data

A scan tool can access two broad kinds of information:

- **Generic OBD-II data** is standardized for emissions-related systems. Key services include **$01** current data, **$02** freeze frame, **$03** stored DTCs, **$06** on-board monitor test results, **$07** pending DTCs, **$09** vehicle information such as VIN and calibration IDs, and **$0A** permanent DTCs.
- **Enhanced (OEM) data** comes from manufacturer-specific software. It offers many more parameters, access to non-engine modules, and **bidirectional controls** that command components on and off.

Generic data works on almost every vehicle; enhanced data usually tells you more.

## Understand DTC status

- **Pending:** The monitor failed once. Many faults require a second failure before the MIL turns on.
- **Confirmed or stored:** The fault met the criteria to turn on the MIL.
- **Permanent:** Cannot be erased with a scan tool. The module clears it after the monitor runs and passes, which helps prove a repair.
- **History:** Many OEMs record past faults with occurrence counters.

## Freeze frame

A freeze frame is a snapshot of key parameters recorded when a DTC set. Typical values include engine RPM, calculated load, coolant temperature, fuel system status, short- and long-term fuel trim, manifold pressure, and vehicle speed.

- Freeze frame shows the **conditions** under which the fault occurred, so you can recreate them for testing and verification.
- In generic OBD-II, misfire and fuel system faults have priority and can replace a freeze frame stored for a lower-priority fault.
- Many OEMs store additional failure records with more parameters.
- **Record freeze frame before clearing codes.** Clearing codes erases it.

## Reading live data effectively

**Know what each value is.** A parameter may be a direct sensor reading, a calculated value, a commanded value, or a **substitute default** that the module uses after a sensor fails. A perfectly steady value that never changes may be a default.

**Compare related values.** Individual numbers rarely prove much; relationships do.

- **After an overnight cold soak**, coolant and intake air temperatures should read close to each other.
- **Key on, engine off**, manifold pressure should read close to barometric pressure.
- **Desired and actual** values, such as cam position, fuel pressure, and idle speed, should track each other.
- **Throttle and pedal position** sensors should agree and move smoothly.

**Improve the data.** Graph values instead of watching numbers, record during road tests, and limit the parameter list to what you need so each value updates faster.

**Use known-good references.** Compare readings with OEM specifications or known-good data from the same vehicle and engine.

## Worked example (illustrative values)

A customer reports hard starting on cold mornings only. The vehicle has sat outside overnight.

- Before starting, intake air temperature reads **8 °C (46 °F)** and coolant temperature reads **31 °C (88 °F)**.
- After a full cold soak, these should be close. An infrared thermometer on the thermostat housing and the outside temperature both agree with the intake air reading.

The coolant sensor is reporting a warmer engine than reality, so the module reduces cold-start enrichment, which matches the complaint. On a typical thermistor circuit, a reading that is too warm means the module sees a signal voltage that is too low, caused either by a sensor whose resistance has drifted low or by a partial short to ground in the signal circuit.

The next test is to measure the sensor's resistance at a known temperature and compare it with the OEM chart. The resistance is far too low for the actual temperature, so the sensor is replaced. The repair is verified the next morning: both temperatures agree after the cold soak, and the engine starts normally.

The scan data pointed to the problem, and a direct measurement proved it.

## Common mistakes

- Clearing codes before saving freeze frame data.
- Judging a single reading without comparing related values.
- Trusting a steady value that may be a substituted default.
- Watching too many parameters at a slow refresh rate and missing a brief dropout.

## Safety

- Road tests with a scan tool need a second person to operate the tool, or a recording made while the driver concentrates on driving.
- Route the scan tool cable so it cannot interfere with the pedals or steering.
- Run engines indoors only with exhaust extraction, and keep clear of belts and fans.

## Key takeaways

- Generic OBD-II data is standardized; enhanced data adds depth and bidirectional control.
- Know whether a code is pending, confirmed, permanent, or history.
- Freeze frame records the conditions when a fault set; save it before clearing codes.
- Compare related values: temperatures after a cold soak, manifold pressure with barometric pressure, desired with actual.
- Use scan data to direct the next test, then prove the fault with a measurement.

lessons.title: Mode $06: on-board monitor test results
lessons.body:
## What Mode $06 shows

OBD-II monitors are self-tests that the engine module runs on emissions-related systems: catalyst efficiency, oxygen sensors, EGR, EVAP, misfire, and others. A DTC tells you only that a test **failed** its limit. **Mode $06**, also called Service $06 or on-board monitoring test results, shows the **actual test value along with the minimum and maximum limits**.

That difference matters. A test that passes by a wide margin and a test that barely passes both show "no code," but Mode $06 lets you see which one you have.

## Why technicians use it

- **Find marginal components** before they set a code, such as a catalyst near its limit or an oxygen sensor responding slowly.
- **Investigate driveability complaints with no codes**, such as a slight idle shake from low-level misfires.
- **Verify repairs** by confirming that the relevant monitor ran again and passed with a healthy margin.

## How the data is organized

On vehicles that use CAN communication for OBD-II, which covers most US vehicles from the 2008 model year onward, Mode $06 data is standardized:

- **Monitor ID (MID):** identifies the monitor, such as a catalyst bank, an oxygen sensor, or a cylinder's misfire data.
- **Test ID (TID):** identifies the specific test within that monitor.
- **Unit and scaling ID:** tells the scan tool how to convert the raw value into readable units.
- **Test value, minimum limit, and maximum limit:** The test passes when the value falls within the limits.

On older, pre-CAN vehicles, many test and component IDs were **manufacturer-defined**, so their meaning must come from OEM information. Even on newer vehicles, some tests are manufacturer-specific. Many scan tools translate IDs into descriptions, but check the OEM information when the meaning is unclear.

## Misfire data

On vehicles that support it, **MIDs $A2 through $AD** report misfire data for cylinders 1 through 12, typically including counts for the current or most recent drive cycle and an average over recent cycles. This makes Mode $06 one of the best places to find a cylinder that misfires occasionally but not often enough to set a code.

## Interpreting results carefully

- Results update only when the monitor **runs**. If the enable conditions have not been met since codes were cleared, the data may be old, empty, or reset.
- Clearing codes or disconnecting the battery can erase results on many vehicles. **Record Mode $06 before clearing anything.**
- Check **which limit applies**. Some tests fail when the value is too high, others when it is too low.
- A value close to its limit is a **clue**, not a verdict. Use it to choose the next test, not to condemn a part.

## Worked example (illustrative values)

A customer reports a slight shake at idle. There is no MIL and no stored or pending code.

- Mode $06 misfire data shows cylinder 4 with a noticeably higher misfire count on the last drive cycle than the other cylinders, which show zero or near zero.
- Enhanced misfire counters confirm cylinder 4 misfires occasionally at idle when the engine is warm.
- Swapping the cylinder 4 coil with cylinder 2 moves the misfires to cylinder 2 on the next idle test.

The coil is replaced, and after a complete drive cycle, Mode $06 shows **zero misfires on all cylinders**. The shake is gone. Without Mode $06, the complaint might have been dismissed because no code was stored.

## Other useful Mode $06 tests

- **Catalyst monitor:** The margin between the test value and the limit shows how close the converter is to failing.
- **Oxygen sensor tests:** Response and switching tests can reveal a slow sensor.
- **EVAP tests:** Leak test results can show a small leak developing before a code sets.
- **EGR tests:** Flow-related tests can show a restricted system.

## Safety

- Collecting fresh Mode $06 data often requires a drive cycle that meets specific enable conditions. Drive safely and legally; have a helper operate the scan tool.
- Idle and running tests require exhaust extraction indoors and clearance from belts and fans.

## Key takeaways

- Mode $06 shows actual test values and limits, not just pass or fail.
- Use it to find marginal components, investigate no-code complaints, and verify repairs.
- CAN-era data is standardized by monitor and test IDs; older and some OEM-specific tests require OEM information.
- MIDs $A2 through $AD report per-cylinder misfire data on supporting vehicles.
- Record Mode $06 before clearing codes, and treat near-limit values as clues for further testing.

lessons.title: Pattern failures versus testing
lessons.body:
## What a pattern failure is

A **pattern failure** is a problem that occurs frequently on a particular model, engine, or component. Technicians learn about patterns from TSBs, OEM training, repair databases that list common fixes, professional forums, and their own experience. Knowing the patterns is valuable. It is one of the main reasons experienced technicians diagnose faster.

The danger is treating a pattern as a diagnosis. **The vehicle in your bay does not know it is supposed to have the common problem.**

## Patterns are probabilities, not proof

Think of a pattern as a head start on the odds.

Suppose that on a certain engine, 60 out of every 100 vehicles with a specific symptom have the known pattern failure. That is useful: the pattern is the most likely cause, so it deserves the first test. But if you replace the part without testing, you are **wrong 40% of the time**. Each wrong guess costs the customer money, delays the real repair, and damages your credibility.

Now add a quick test that almost always fails when the pattern part is bad and almost always passes when it is good. After a failing result, the probability that the pattern part is at fault approaches certainty. After a passing result, you have saved the cost of an unneeded part and eliminated a major suspect. Either way, **the test paid for itself.**

This is the logic behind probability-based diagnostic tools: the pattern sets the starting likelihood, and each test result updates it.

## Using patterns well

1. **Check the match.** Does the vehicle match the pattern exactly: engine, model year range, codes, symptoms, conditions, and mileage? A near match is weaker evidence.
2. **Find the quickest confirming test.** Many patterns have a known test, such as a swap test, a specific data value, or a visual check.
3. **Look for evidence that does not fit.** If something contradicts the pattern, investigate it rather than ignoring it.
4. **Ask why the part failed.** Some patterns have underlying causes, such as coils damaged by worn spark plugs, or repeated alternator failures caused by a bad battery or high-resistance cables.
5. **Verify the repair** under the conditions that caused the original complaint.

## When testing seems expensive

Occasionally, testing a part costs more than replacing it, for example with an inexpensive, easily accessible part that is due for maintenance anyway. Replacing it can be a reasonable **business decision**, but only when it is explained to the customer, agreed to, and documented as a decision, not presented as a diagnosis. If the symptom remains, the diagnosis continues.

## Worked example

A vehicle arrives with **P0303**, a cylinder 3 misfire. This engine is known for ignition coil failures, and the pattern points strongly to the coil.

- **Quick confirming test:** The cylinder 3 coil is swapped with cylinder 1. After running the engine, the misfire **stays on cylinder 3**. The pattern is not confirmed.
- The cylinder 3 spark plug looks normal and similar to the others.
- A scope on the cylinder 3 injector control circuit shows **missing injector pulses**, which become more frequent when the harness connector is gently moved.
- The connector has a corroded, loose terminal.

The terminal is repaired, and misfire counters stay at zero during a road test under the freeze frame conditions. Following the pattern without testing would have produced a new coil, the same misfire, and an unhappy customer.

## The cost of guessing

- **Parts that were not needed**, often not returnable once installed
- **Comebacks**, which cost labor and reputation
- **New problems** introduced by unnecessary disassembly
- **Lost learning**: guessing teaches nothing, while testing builds the experience that makes future diagnosis faster

## Safety

- Confirming tests often involve running the engine. Use exhaust extraction indoors, set the parking brake, and keep clear of belts and fans.
- Verification road tests should be driven safely, with a helper operating the scan tool.

## Key takeaways

- Pattern failures raise the probability of a cause; they do not prove it.
- Use patterns to decide which test to perform first.
- A quick confirming test protects the customer and your credibility, whether it passes or fails.
- Ask why a pattern part failed, and repair the underlying cause.
- Replacing a part without testing is at most a documented, customer-approved decision, never a diagnosis.

quiz.title: Diagnostic Strategy and Scan Data Quiz

questions.q: An engine cranks at normal speed but will not start. Scan data shows 0 RPM while cranking. Where should you focus first?
choices: The fuel pump
The crankshaft position signal and its circuit
The spark plugs
Cylinder compression
questions.explanation: If the module does not see engine rotation, it typically will not fire coils or injectors. The missing RPM signal points to the crankshaft position sensor, its circuit, or its reluctor before fuel, spark, or mechanical checks.

questions.q: Before performing a test, a technician asks, 'Would a different result change my next step?' Why is this a useful question?
choices: It lets you skip repair verification
It helps you choose the most expensive test first
It ensures every test is invasive enough to be conclusive
It helps avoid tests whose results would not change the plan
questions.explanation: A test is only valuable if its possible results lead to different actions. If every outcome leads to the same next step, the test can wait while a more informative test is performed.

questions.q: A freeze frame shows coolant temperature at -40 °C (-40 °F) while the engine was running at normal RPM on a mild day. What does this most likely indicate?
choices: An open in the coolant temperature sensor circuit
The engine really was at -40 °C
A thermostat stuck open
A short to ground in the sensor signal circuit
questions.explanation: On a typical thermistor circuit, an open pulls the signal voltage high, which the module reads as extremely cold. A short to ground pulls the signal low and reads as extremely hot. A thermostat stuck open causes slow warm-up, not an impossible reading.

questions.q: After an overnight cold soak, the intake air temperature and an infrared thermometer agree, but coolant temperature reads much warmer. What is the best next step?
choices: Replace the thermostat
Replace the intake air temperature sensor
Test the coolant temperature sensor and its circuit against the OEM temperature chart
Clear the codes and recheck tomorrow
questions.explanation: Two independent references agree, so the coolant temperature reading is suspect. Measuring the sensor and circuit against the OEM chart proves whether the sensor or the wiring is at fault before any part is replaced.

questions.q: After a verified repair, a permanent DTC remains stored. What clears it?
choices: Clearing codes with a scan tool
The module, after the related monitor runs and passes
Disconnecting the battery overnight
Reprogramming the module
questions.explanation: Permanent DTCs cannot be erased with a scan tool or by disconnecting power. The module clears them after the monitor runs and passes, which helps show the repair was effective.

questions.q: Mode $06 shows a catalyst monitor result that is within its limits but close to the failure limit. No code is stored. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: The catalyst has failed and must be replaced
The data is invalid because no code is stored
Mode $06 cannot be used for catalyst monitors
The catalyst is passing but marginal, a clue to investigate rather than a reason to condemn it
questions.explanation: A near-limit result is useful information, but it is a passing result. Look for causes that could affect converter efficiency, such as misfires or fuel control problems, and monitor the trend.

questions.q: A customer reports a slight idle shake. There is no MIL and no pending or stored code. Which information is likely to help most?
choices: Per-cylinder misfire data in Mode $06
The VIN from Mode $09
Readiness monitor status only
Freeze frame data
questions.explanation: Mode $06 misfire data, reported by MIDs $A2 through $AD on supporting vehicles, can reveal a cylinder with low-level misfires that have not set a code. Freeze frame requires a stored code.

questions.q: On a certain engine, about 60 of every 100 vehicles with a particular symptom have a known pattern failure. If you replace that part on every such vehicle without testing, how often will you be wrong?
choices: Never
About 6% of the time
About 40% of the time
About 60% of the time
questions.explanation: The pattern covers 60% of cases, so the other 40% have a different cause. A quick confirming test avoids those wrong repairs.

questions.q: An engine known for ignition coil failures has a cylinder 3 misfire. After swapping coils, the misfire stays on cylinder 3. What should you conclude?
choices: The coil is still the most likely cause
The coil is unlikely, so continue with plug, injector circuit, and mechanical tests
Replace all coils as a set
Swap tests are not valid on this engine
questions.explanation: The swap test result outweighs the pattern. A misfire that stays with the cylinder points to something else serving that cylinder.

questions.q: Why should you limit the number of parameters displayed when recording scan data for an intermittent fault?
choices: It lowers the module's operating temperature
OBD-II regulations require it
It prevents DTCs from setting during the test
Fewer parameters update faster, making brief dropouts easier to catch
questions.explanation: Data link bandwidth is shared among the parameters requested. Selecting only the relevant parameters increases the update rate, so short glitches are less likely to be missed.
